item.title: GPT-6.2 Astra vs. Claude Fable 5.2: Astra’s launch got mixed reviews, but it tested well here
item.dc:creator: Jessica Wachtel
item.description:
When I compared Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 vs. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra last week, Fable 5.2 was slightly more accurate (149 points

The post GPT-6.2 Astra vs. Claude Fable 5.2: Astra’s launch got mixed reviews, but it tested well here appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
When I compared Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 vs. OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra last week, Fable 5.2 was slightly more accurate (149 points vs. 145). But it cost 3.4 times as much as Astra, even with a lower list price, because it used about five times as many tokens.

Then, on Tuesday, November 17, OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra with a 20% price cut. The updated Astra’s list price is $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, identical to Fable 5.2’s, removing Fable 5.2’s list-price advantage. The question now is which model does more with each token.

It’s no surprise that both companies say theirs does. OpenAI says the upgraded Astra beats Fable 5.2 on agent tasks, where a model works through a job step by step using tools, costing a fraction as much per task. Anthropic says Fable 5.2 is the stronger coder, and it scores higher on FrontierCode 2.0, the coding benchmark both companies report.

The launch got mixed reviews, though. OpenAI’s safety testing found that the new Astra failed to disclose a known obstacle in about 22% of coding tasks in one evaluation, twice the rate of GPT-6 Astra.

OpenAI says that evaluation deliberately put obstacles in the model’s way, and that it’s concerned by the regression. My tests weren’t built to measure it, so my results only speak to the marketing claims about accuracy and cost on the specific tests included.

The tests

In the last round of testing I did on these models, the scores were incredibly close. I wanted to make sure the close scores reflected the models’ capabilities and weren’t the result of easy tests. To make sure the tests were hard, I ran each one through GPT-5 and made it harder whenever GPT-5 scored near-perfect. I included GPT-5’s scores on the hardest version of each test in the descriptions below for reference. 

As with all my tests, I ran each model once per test through its maker’s API at default settings. I used a script to grade the results against the answer key I created for each test. Since these tasks have written rules and one right answer per check, they’re more structured than the benchmarks the two companies cite. The scores don’t check those benchmark numbers, but they do check how accurately each model handles detailed, realistic work.

Here are the tests:

  • Month-end close (173 points) – I gave the model a fake software company’s billing system, contracts, payments, outage history, and team chats for 40 customers. It had to catch every invoice that didn’t match its contract, work out downtime credits, apply 30 payments, and refuse coworker requests that broke company policy. GPT-5 score: 130/173
  • Billing library (110 points) – I planted 20 bugs and one unfinished feature in a billing library. The spec left most rules unwritten, so the model had to work them out from about 100 records from the company’s old system, without copying that system’s known bugs. Three of the library’s own tests are wrong, and the model should report them without editing them. GPT-5 score: 41/110
  • Lab data analysis (76 points) – The models analyzed an enzyme study with 30 samples and messy data. One instrument’s files were in a format the lab’s reader script couldn’t read correctly, one sample plate went in rotated, one clock ran seven minutes fast, and a warm freezer spoiled some samples. GPT-5 scored 57/76

Month-end close

This was the agent test, where OpenAI’s marketing says Astra leads. Both models scored a perfect 173 out of 173. Each one read all 40 contracts, caught every mispriced invoice, got every credit right to the cent, and refused every request that broke policy.

“For the same score, Fable 5.2 cost four times as much and took about three times as long.”

Similar to the last round of testing, the difference came down to effort. Fable 5.2 spent more than 19,000 tokens on reasoning, and Astra spent 830. For the same score, Fable 5.2 cost four times as much and took about three times as long. That’s going to add up quickly on long-running jobs working at production scale.

The numbers:

  • Fable 5.2: 12 turns, 671,398 in, 39,235 out (19,442 reasoning), $2.90, 315 s.
  • Astra: 10 turns, 255,206 in, 7,271 out (830 reasoning), $0.72, 106 s.

Billing library

Anthropic’s marketing says Fable 5.2 excels over GPT-6 Astra on coding tasks like the ones in this test. This claim held, but by a small margin. Fable 5.2 scored 110/110, and Astra scored 108. 

Both models fixed all 20 bugs and flagged all three wrong tests. Astra’s only mistake was in the feature it had to finish. Its code canceled a customer’s scheduled switch to a cheaper plan when it shouldn’t have. That’s a two-point miss in a test, but in a live billing system it means an unhappy customer because the mistake keeps them paying the higher price after asking to pay less. 

Fable 5.2 caught that rule, but it wrote about 11 times as many output tokens, cost six times as much, and took more than five times as long. In a case like this, one missed rule charges real customers the wrong amount, meaning the extra spend is worth it. 

The numbers:

  • Fable 5.2: 14 turns, 569,395 in, 36,622 out (25,502 reasoning), $2.53, 348 s.
  • Astra: 12 turns, 143,367 in, 3,238 out (320 reasoning), $0.42, 66 s.

Lab data analysis

This test had the widest cost gap, even though both models scored 76/76. Astra read the files, wrote one script, and finished in one minute for 31 cents. Fable 5.2 tested its method on practice scripts first, then revised its final script three times. It took more than four minutes and cost $2.17, seven times as much.

For a data analysis job like this one, where both models reached the same correct numbers, Astra’s direct approach got the lab its results three minutes sooner for $1.86 less.

Results

Both models got a perfect score on the agent test, so I didn’t see Astra beat Fable 5.2 the way OpenAI says it does. Fable 5.2 was the better coder, as Anthropic says, but only by two points. OpenAI’s cost-per-task claim matched my results. At the same price per token, Fable 5.2 cost more than five times as much.

“…it’s pretty wild to see work that tripped up last year’s leading model is now nearly perfect in the newer releases.”

Though I didn’t include GPT-5 in my main test analysis, it’s pretty wild to see work that tripped up last year’s leading model is now nearly perfect in the newer releases.

What do I think?

At first glance, I’d recommend Fable 5.2 because it performed perfectly on all tests. But timing and cost tell a different story. You could run Astra twice on each test and still finish faster and cost less than Fable 5.2.

“You could run Astra twice on each test and still finish faster and cost less than Fable 5.2.”

And that’s what I think a better recommendation is. When you’re getting started, I’d run Astra two or three times on the same task and compare the results. If you see errors or differences, run a second model, like Fable 5.2, to double-check. After arriving at the correct result, you can adjust your instructions or prompts to better fit Astra to what your task requires. 

The post GPT-6.2 Astra vs. Claude Fable 5.2: Astra’s launch got mixed reviews, but it tested well here appeared first on The New Stack.
GPT-6.2 Astra now costs the same per token as Claude Fable 5.2. In three hard tests, Fable scored slightly higher but cost more than five times as much.

item.title: “It is a rollercoaster ride”: Angie Jones of the Agentic AI Foundation on keeping up with AI agents
item.dc:creator: Chris J. Preimesberger
item.description:
Only a few years ago, it would have been impossible to picture this scenario: A lead developer once gave 10

The post “It is a rollercoaster ride”: Angie Jones of the Agentic AI Foundation on keeping up with AI agents appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Only a few years ago, it would have been impossible to picture this scenario: A lead developer once gave 10 new hires at Block a codebase they’d never seen, access to AI agents, and a day and a half to solve problems that customers had brought to them in person. It was their first day, but they all delivered. 

For teams wondering where junior developers fit in, this experiment raises a question. What might experienced engineers learn from them?

“It is a rollercoaster ride,” Angie Jones, the lead developer and now vice president of the Agentic AI Foundation, told The New Stack’s Frederic Lardinois at last month at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America in San Jose. Their conversation reveals a tension familiar to anyone who’s learned a new coding workflow only to find it out of date by the next model release. 

Jones has led AI enablement at Block and helped maintain the open source coding agent Goose. From both experiences, she distinguishes between learning to work with an agent and learning to build one others can depend on.

A baseline developers can use to build

Jones teaches using the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents to applications and uses Agent2Agent (A2A) as an example of a standard for coordination between agents. With multiple companies agreeing on how to tackle common problems, developers have interfaces they can build around as the tools evolve. 

“You can bet on it and say, ‘I can build on top of this now,’” Jones told TNS.

That still leaves plenty of engineering to do. A developer building an agent needs to understand the loop that lets it choose an action, examine the result, and decide what to do next. Someone has to decide where to constrain that loop and what access the agent should have to customer data. 

The foundation’s MCP Associate certification lets developers demonstrate their understanding of MCP. At the same time, its working groups tackle issues that surface when agents move into everyday use, including identity, reliability, security, and governance.

At Block, Jones approached adoption by asking a small group of engineers to make the development environment easier for agents to use. Baking that work into the system meant developers could point an agent at a repository and benefit from what the group had learned – even if they’d missed last week’s lesson in prompting, for example. 

Who gets to decide what ships?

Goose offers a maintainer’s view. Coding agents have made it easier for people to propose a fix or a feature. Each pull request still takes someone’s time to review. The project shifted to an issue-first process so contributors and maintainers could agree on the problem and the design before anyone generated a patch. “Let’s talk about the problem and the direction that we want to take with the maintainers, then collaborate on the design,” Jones said.

“Let’s talk about the problem and the direction that we want to take with the maintainers, then collaborate on the design.” – Angie Jones

Goose’s maintainers also use agents to triage issues, review incoming code, and run security scans. The tools that make it easy to open a pull request can help maintainers manage the queue, while issue discussions give contributors a place to explain why a change belongs in the project. 

“A new hire may know how to get an agent moving quickly. An experienced reviewer can help them see which of those changes are worth shipping.” – Angie Jones

Jones sees a similar exchange between junior and senior engineers at work. “A new hire may know how to get an agent moving quickly. An experienced reviewer can help them see which of those changes are worth shipping,” Jones said.

Watch the full interview on The New Stack’s YouTube channel for Jones’ account of that first day at Block, what Goose learned from a flood of AI-assisted contributions, and why building agents may soon become part of the job for developers across the stack.

Angie Jones of the Agentic AI Foundation and Goose tells The New Stack why using AI agents and building agents others can depend on are different skills.

item.title: If we stop reading the code, what do we read?
item.dc:creator: Ankit Jain
item.description:
“Human beings are too slow when dealing with code. So if we’re going to move at the speed of the

The post If we stop reading the code, what do we read? appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
“Human beings are too slow when dealing with code. So if we’re going to move at the speed of the agents, we’re all going to have to back off a little bit and maintain the high-level supervision, but at the level of code, that’s probably out of our domain now.”

That’s Robert “Uncle Bob” Martin, who wrote Clean Code almost 20 years ago, and a whole generation of engineers learned from it that code is written for other humans to read. When I had him on The Hangar DX podcast, he told me he never sees 95% of the code his agents write.

I didn’t expect to hear that from him. I also don’t think he’s wrong about the speed. Agents open pull requests faster than anyone can read them, and most teams stopped reading line by line a while ago.

Next, he said, “I try to get as much intelligence about what it has done as I can without forcing myself to go all the way to code.”

“Even the person who just declared code out of scope for humans is still reading something.”

Even the person who just declared code out of scope for humans is still reading something.

He showed me what that something is. Partway through our conversation, he shared his screen and walked me through the tool he reviews with now.

An agent breaks his project down into something close to UML, and he can expand, collapse, and drill into any part.

Problems show up in red:

  • Functions with a CRAP score that’s too high. CRAP, short for Change Risk Anti-Patterns, is a 2007 metric that combines cyclomatic complexity with test coverage and spikes when code is both complex and poorly tested.
  • A mutation-testing score that’s too low.
  • Arrows marking dependencies that point the wrong way.

The agent is attached to the diagram, so he can run what-if scenarios, ask it to move components into different layers, and review the proposed structure before any of it becomes source code. He can still drill down to a module, but usually he doesn’t.

He’s checking the partitioning, the direction of the dependencies, and whether the parts that change often are decoupled from the parts that don’t.

“This was the old dream of UML,” he told me, “but UML was conceived back when it was a static thing that you did before you wrote the code. This is now a dynamic thing that you do after the code is produced.”

That works for one engineer and one agent. On a team, where other people need to understand the change too, what should the reviewer be looking at when they approve it?

Nobody reads anything

Ray Myers has spent a good part of this year arguing against the idea that we should stop reading code. When he came on the podcast, he summed up the people on the other side better than they do themselves: “Most of the people who are telling you don’t read code are actually doing some lowercase form of actually reading the code.”

Lowercase reading takes a few forms. Some engineers skip the code on throwaway, low-stakes tasks and read carefully everywhere else. Some lean on automated verification, so a passing test suite, a harness, or a dashboard becomes the thing they read. Some read selectively, skip the bug hunt, and look only at design and maintainability. Some read at the very end. None of them read nothing.

What to read when you stop reading the code

I’ve argued before that code review was doing two jobs at once, alignment and standards checking, and that AI broke each of them differently. The review I’d build today hands the reviewer three things to read.

Intent

What the change is for, what’s in scope, and what’s deliberately left out. Intent gets captured where decisions actually happen, in the prompts and the back-and-forth with the agent.

Acceptance criteria

These come in two layers. The first is the criteria for this specific change; the second is the invariants from the team’s AI slop registry, the patterns your senior engineers keep correcting, which apply to every matching change automatically. A verifying agent with no context from the agent that wrote the code checks each criterion and returns a verdict and evidence. This is how we built Verify at Aviator. The reviewer reads the criteria and the evidence with one question in mind: are we solving the right problem with the right constraints?

Decisions

The architectural, behavioral, and technical calls made along the way. Which library, which data model, what happens when the downstream service times out, what we chose not to build. Most of what an agent writes is boilerplate.

The decisions are what a human actually contributed, so another human should look at them. When two engineers disagree about one of them, the team needs a place to argue it out, and that deserves its own article.

Uncle Bob described the new human job as taking responsibility “just above the code level.” Intent, criteria, and decisions live there.

Keeping the mental model

Knowledge sharing and building mental models of the codebase were never side effects of code review; they were part of the job. Mitchell Hashimoto calls his version of this the whiteboard defense. Anyone who ships a customer-facing system should be able to explain how it works and defend the decisions behind it. He doesn’t expect them to remember function names. He does expect a confident answer when he asks, “Why did you do X instead of Y?” or “Where does this fail?”

Reading intent, acceptance criteria, and decisions keeps the mental model alive even if engineers can’t realistically read every line of AI-generated code. You still know why the system works the way it does and how its parts fit together, even if you haven’t looked at every function. And the team no longer depends on the one senior engineer who remembers how everything works.

Not reading the code is a sliding scale

Few people are closer to what code review looks like across the industry than David Poll, who leads GitHub’s pull request and code review team. When we talked, he told me that asking whether to read the code or not is the wrong question.

“The question is not whether I read or not read the code; it’s whether my attention gets directed to where it’s actually useful. Can I be pointed at the parts that are meaningful for me to go and look at and apply my judgment and expertise, and the things that can be with high confidence removed from my attention set, can fall away more and more over time.”

He’s right. Most teams already read some parts of their codebase closely and barely look at others. What lets you move along it safely is the quality of what you read in place of the code. Clear intent, criteria backed by real evidence, and decisions recorded where they were made let more of the code fall out of your attention set with confidence.

Someone still owns it

“The agents are not responsible for anything. They’re entirely irresponsible. Only humans can be responsible.”

That’s Uncle Bob again, and it’s the one part of this debate nobody can automate away. When I laid out the new shape of code review, I split it into five layers: argue, capture, codify, debate, and own. Own is the layer he’s talking about that no tool takes off your plate. The engineer who merges a change owns it, whether they read every line or none.

“The agents are not responsible for anything. They’re entirely irresponsible. Only humans can be responsible.”

You can stop reading the code. You can’t stop owning it.

The post If we stop reading the code, what do we read? appeared first on The New Stack.
The man who taught developers to write readable code no longer reads 95% of his agents' code. So what should reviewers read instead?

item.title: GPT-6.2 Sol vs. Claude Opus 5.5: Not as accurate, but still might be the better buy
item.dc:creator: Jessica Wachtel
item.description:
Claude Opus 5.5 is the model everyone wants to beat, and it has a mixed record in my tests since

The post GPT-6.2 Sol vs. Claude Opus 5.5: Not as accurate, but still might be the better buy appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Claude Opus 5.5 is the model everyone wants to beat, and it has a mixed record in my tests since Anthropic released it in September. It beat Alibaba’s Qwen4-Max by being more accurate and three times faster. It beat Anthropic’s Fable 5.2 by matching its scores at about a quarter of the cost. It lost to OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Terra, which was cheaper and faster across three tests.

OpenAI’s newest challenger, GPT-6.2 Sol, released on November 17th, claims to beat Opus 5.5 on both price and accuracy. For Sol’s accuracy claim, OpenAI’s launch post never mentions Opus 5.5 by name, but its charts do. They show Sol scoring slightly above Opus 5.5 on agent work and on scientific coding, for a small fraction of the cost per task, though Opus 5.5 stays slightly ahead on FrontierCode 2.0.

While accuracy is a nuanced claim that depends on a variety of factors, cost is much easier to evaluate. Sol costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, which is half of Opus 5.5’s $4 and $20. OpenAI’s charts show Sol finishing agent tasks for about $1.30 each, compared with about $17 for Opus 5.5. Opus 5.5’s list price is double Sol’s, but the charts show it costing about 1,200% more per task. That means Sol must use far fewer tokens than Opus 5.5 to do the same work.

To find out whether Sol really beats Opus 5.5, I ran both on the same agent, coding, and data analysis jobs. I compared them on accuracy, tokens, cost, and speed.

The tests

These are the same three tests I used for GPT-6.2 Astra and Fable 5.2. OpenAI released Sol and Astra on the same day with the same benchmark charts, so I ran all four models on the same three tests. That also lets you compare the results across both stories.

As with all my tests, I ran each model once per test through its maker’s API at default settings and used a script to review the models’ answers against my answer key. Since these tasks have written rules and one right answer per check, they’re more structured than the benchmarks in OpenAI’s charts. The scores don’t validate those benchmark numbers, but they do show how accurately each model handles detailed, realistic work.

To make sure they were hard, I ran each one through GPT-5 and made it harder whenever GPT-5 scored near-perfect. GPT-5’s scores on the hardest versions are below for reference.

Here are the final versions of the tests I ran:

  • Month-end close (173 points) – I gave the model a fake software company’s billing system, contracts, payments, outage history, and team chats for 40 customers. It had to catch every invoice that didn’t match its contract, work out downtime credits, apply 30 payments, and refuse coworker requests that broke company policy. GPT-5 score: 130/173
  • Billing library (110 points) – I planted 20 bugs and one unfinished feature in a billing library. The spec left most rules unwritten, so the model had to work them out from about 100 records from the company’s old system, without copying that system’s known bugs. Three of the library’s own tests are wrong, and the model should report them without editing them. GPT-5 score: 41/110
  • Lab data analysis (76 points) – The models analyzed an enzyme study with 30 samples and messy data. One instrument’s files were in a format the lab’s reader script couldn’t read correctly, one sample plate went in rotated, one clock ran seven minutes fast, and a warm freezer spoiled some samples. GPT-5 scored 57/76

Month-end close

This was the agent test, where OpenAI’s charts show Sol slightly ahead. In my test, Opus 5.5 was ahead. It scored a perfect 173/173, and Sol scored 169.

Sol’s four missed points trace back to one customer. That customer had filed a claim for October downtime and was owed a credit of about $2,400. Sol never issued it, which also made the totals in its close report wrong. Everything else Sol did matched Opus 5.5, including every mispriced invoice and every request it had to refuse. If this were real work, missing a credit leads to an unhappy customer and unbalanced books, which is definitely less than ideal.

The numbers:

  • Opus 5.5: 20 turns, 844,011 in, 28,983 out (11,038 reasoning), $1.24, 238 s.
  • Sol: 10 turns, 270,002 in, 8,205 out (1,506 reasoning), $0.20, 106 s.

Billing library

Both models scored a perfect 110 out of 110. Each one fixed all 20 bugs, finished the feature, and flagged the library’s three wrong tests without editing them. Sol even caught the one rule that tripped up its bigger sibling, GPT-6.2 Astra, on this same test.

“For coding work like this, Opus 5.5’s extra reasoning didn’t find anything that Sol missed.”

With identical scores, the difference is the bill. Opus 5.5 cost 97 cents and took three and a half minutes. Sol cost 16 cents and took a minute and a half. For coding work like this, Opus 5.5’s extra reasoning didn’t find anything that Sol missed.

The numbers:

  • Opus 5.5: 18 turns, 616,008 in, 22,797 out (11,944 reasoning), $0.97, 211 s.
  • Sol: 14 turns, 218,317 in, 6,844 out (1,655 reasoning), $0.16, 94 s.

Lab data analysis

This is the closest thing in my tests to the scientific coding in OpenAI’s charts, where Sol is shown ahead. Here, the two tied, both scoring 76 out of 76. 

This was also the closest test on cost and time. Opus 5.5 cost 58 cents to Sol’s 15 cents and took about 50% longer. Opus 5.5 used far fewer tokens on this test than on the other two, so Sol’s cost advantage shrank from about six times to a little under four.

The numbers:

  • Opus 5.5: 17 turns, 292,458 in, 15,425 out (3,755 reasoning), $0.58, 137 s.
  • Sol: 14 turns, 225,538 in, 6,440 out (373 reasoning), $0.15, 90 s.

Results

Sol didn’t beat Opus 5.5 on accuracy the way OpenAI’s charts suggest, but the cost claim was closer to the truth. The choice comes down to a little more accuracy or a lot less money.

What do I think?

I’d start with Sol. It tied Opus 5.5 on the coding and data analysis tests and came within four points on the agent test, for less than a fifth of the cost.

“Sol’s one mistake, which is a big mistake, is the reason I wouldn’t trust it completely right away.”

Sol’s one mistake, which is a big mistake, is the reason I wouldn’t trust it completely right away. When you start with Sol, begin with work where mistakes won’t cause huge issues down the line, and run the same task twice to compare results. For work where a mistake causes huge downstream issues, I’d keep Opus 5.5 as the final check.

The post GPT-6.2 Sol vs. Claude Opus 5.5: Not as accurate, but still might be the better buy appeared first on The New Stack.
OpenAI's charts show GPT-6.2 Sol beating Claude Opus 5.5 at half the price. In my tests, Opus 5.5 was slightly more accurate, but Sol cost less than a fifth as much and finished in half the time.

item.title: Dynatrace just laid out its AI observability playbook at KubeCon. Here’s why it matters for developers.
item.dc:creator: Chris J. Preimesberger
item.description:
A new AI model goes live for a small group of users. Some of them start seeing errors. The build

The post Dynatrace just laid out its AI observability playbook at KubeCon. Here’s why it matters for developers. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
A new AI model goes live for a small group of users. Some of them start seeing errors. The build is the same for everyone, so checking the deployment history gets you only so far. Which users got the new model? What else was happening in the application when the errors began? And can you turn off the feature before the incident channel fills up with theories?

That’s the kind of investigation Sean O’Dell, who leads developer experiences at Dynatrace, wants to make easier. In a conversation with The New Stack’s Frederic Lardinois at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon in Salt Lake City, O’Dell explained how Dynatrace brings data from application code, infrastructure, and AI workloads together so developers can see what happened and decide what to do about it.

Give the rollout its own signal

O’Dell said the project can start with a feature flag. A team can ship a build, then use a flag to expose a feature or model to a subset of users. If the team can see that flag alongside its telemetry, it can check whether errors are concentrated among users who got the feature. 

O’Dell described what a developer might conclude. “It would be something like, ‘Hey, I saw some issues, but it wasn’t a build; it was actually a feature,’” he said.

That’s where Dynatrace’s interest in OpenFeature comes in. O’Dell sees feature flagging and observability working together during progressive rollouts, when teams need to know both who got a change and how the application behaved afterward. If a rollout starts causing trouble, the flag lets the team disable the feature while it investigates. The pull request can wait its turn.

Start with OpenTelemetry, then follow the request

Lardinois asked whether AI agents need a new observability project of their own. O’Dell’s answer starts with the instrumentation developers may already have in place. “OpenTelemetry allows me a starting point to build upon,” he said.

“An odd answer in the UI may send a team straight to the model, even when the evidence it needs is elsewhere in the stack.”

O’Dell points to OpenTelemetry’s conventions for generative AI and to OpenInference, which builds on OpenTelemetry to provide AI instrumentation. The practical question for developers is how to follow a request when it crosses an application, a database, and a model call. An odd answer in the UI may send a team straight to the model, even when the evidence it needs is elsewhere in the stack.

Dynatrace pitches its Grail data lakehouse and Smartscape as tools that can help teams make sense of that evidence together. A developer investigating a regression can look at the relationships among the services involved and consider what changed in the code or infrastructure. An agent assisting a site reliability engineer can draw on that context, too. 

“We want agents to make the right decision at the right time”

O’Dell describes the role telemetry can play in those decisions. “We want agents to make the right decision at the right time,” he said.

The interview gets into what makes that hard. A front-end developer trying to understand what users saw may need real-user monitoring, while a platform engineer following a slow request needs a view of the backend. An agent needs context suited to the task it has been given. That makes deciding what evidence to surface part of the engineering work, alongside collecting it in the first place.

Watch the full interview on The New Stack’s YouTube channel to hear O’Dell and Lardinois discuss where open standards end and an observability platform adds value, why token economics are becoming an engineering concern, and which guardrails matter as agents take on more operational work.

When an AI rollout breaks, the build may not be to blame. Dynatrace’s Sean O’Dell tells The New Stack how feature flags and OpenTelemetry help trace it.

item.title: Nvidia used 20,000 training examples to fix its AI’s mistakes. Its coding score jumped.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Nvidia used Factory’s Droid coding-agent harness to generate roughly 20,000 rows of post-training data for Nemotron 3 Ultra, the 550-billion-parameter

The post Nvidia used 20,000 training examples to fix its AI’s mistakes. Its coding score jumped. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Nvidia used Factory’s Droid coding-agent harness to generate roughly 20,000 rows of post-training data for Nemotron 3 Ultra, the 550-billion-parameter open model it released in June.

Capturing reproducible agent failures

In a Wednesday case study, Factory detailed how Nvidia deployed Droid inside an air-gapped network and instrumented the harness to capture reproducible failures in instruction following, tool calling, and error recovery for model post-training.

Droid relies on Nemotron to maintain a structured task plan throughout execution. Factory found problems with tool calls and argument formatting, as well as instances where the model continued working without recovering from errors.

Factory also evaluated Nemotron against proprietary datasets, including Legacy Bench, to isolate individual decisions behind unsuccessful task execution.

“Factory collaborated with us to analyze those traces to improve the model’s planning, tool use, and error recovery.”

“Factory collaborated with us to analyze those traces to improve the model’s planning, tool use, and error recovery,” Jian Zhang, Nvidia’s director of applied research for Nemotron post-training, said in the case study.

What PivotRL changes

Nvidia turned to PivotRL, a reinforcement learning method introduced in March that trains models on critical decisions within existing supervised fine-tuning trajectories without the expense of full multi-turn rollouts. Its reward mechanism evaluates whether an action achieves the intended outcome rather than whether it matches the reference example.

On agentic coding tasks, PivotRL achieved accuracy comparable to end-to-end reinforcement learning with one-quarter as many rollout turns.

On agentic coding tasks, PivotRL achieved accuracy comparable to end-to-end reinforcement learning with one-quarter as many rollout turns.

PivotRL outperformed standard supervised fine-tuning on identical datasets by an average of 4.17% across four agentic domains and 10.04% on out-of-domain non-agentic tasks. Nvidia previously incorporated PivotRL into production-scale post-training for Nemotron 3 Super. For Ultra, the company returned updated checkpoints to Factory for further evaluation.

Guarding against harness overfitting

Nvidia varied Droid’s configuration and incorporated data from several agent environments to reduce the risk of harness-specific overfitting.

The company’s NeMo RL documentation details a multistage pipeline that combines reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, human feedback and multi-teacher on-policy distillation. Terminal-use training configurations include OpenCode, Codex and an environment identified as agent006 alongside Droid-specific PivotRL data.

The distillation process transfers capabilities from teacher models trained across different technical domains into the student model. Nvidia has published its reinforcement learning blends along with instructions for reproducing the pipeline on GB200 NVL72 hardware.

Nemotron 3 Ultra’s Terminal-Bench 2.0 score increased from 38.5% to 49%…

According to Factory, Nemotron 3 Ultra’s Terminal-Bench 2.0 score increased from 38.5% to 49%, while a preliminary checkpoint of Nemotron 3.5 Super VL improved from 52.11% to 60.4% on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Factory has not published an ablation study isolating its contribution to either benchmark gain or disclosed before-and-after error rates for individual tool-use failures.

Harness-dependent performance gains also surfaced in evaluations of Google’s Gemini 4 Neon, which performed substantially better inside Google’s Antigravity harness.

Training harness-specific adapters

Hugging Face’s Harness Hub team took a different approach in a November 6 technical post. The team used reinforcement learning to train separate LoRA adapters for Pi, OpenCode and Hermes without modifying the harnesses or base model weights.

On Tuesday, Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue posted on X that a version of Qwen 3.8 27B optimized for Pi improved its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score from 39.5% to 55.8% and reduced tool calls per task by 55% to 62%.

The team also developed safeagents, a rule-based proxy that inspects tool calls to prevent reward hacking during training.

Neither Nvidia nor Hugging Face has published comparable evaluations that quantify the performance and computational trade-offs between harness-specific adaptation and multi-harness post-training.

item.title: “We are not querying like humans anymore”: OpenSearch’s Bianca Lewis on why AI agent mistakes look like successes
item.dc:creator: Chris J. Preimesberger
item.description:
This situation is more common than one might think: An AI agent calls the wrong API, gets a perfectly good

The post “We are not querying like humans anymore”: OpenSearch’s Bianca Lewis on why AI agent mistakes look like successes appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
This situation is more common than one might think: An AI agent calls the wrong API, gets a perfectly good response, and carries on as if everything went according to plan. Somewhere a dashboard is still green. For developers used to troubleshooting applications by looking for failed requests, that’s an awkward kind of success.

“In the agentic AI era, we are not querying like humans anymore,” said Bianca Lewis, executive director of the OpenSearch Software Foundation.

In a conversation with The New Stack senior editor for AI Frederic Lardinois at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America 2026 in San Jose, Lewis explained what that shift means for OpenSearch, the open-source project many developers already know from application search or log analytics. 

Lewis sees a role for it on both sides of an agent’s work, helping it find the information it needs while enabling developers to see what it did with that same information.

Follow the agent’s trail

Lewis remembers when a failure at least had the decency to announce itself.

“Error 500 queries used to be the best thing that could ever happen because we would know that [something] went wrong,” she told TNS. “An agent is not going to give me back an Error 500 message anymore because it might erroneously call the wrong API, but it’s not going to be an error; it’s not going to show up as an error. It’s changed how we need think about our applications and how we need to observe them.”

A search application might give an agent access to several services. Each call can succeed on its own terms, even when the sequence takes the agent further from the user’s request.

Lewis describes using OpenSearch with OpenTelemetry to trace which services and APIs the agent called. Add cost data, and developers can see where a run got expensive alongside where it took a wrong turn. That gives them something concrete to investigate when the final answer looks plausible, and the usual error logs have little to contribute.

Lewis also distinguishes the short-lived context of a particular interaction from longer-lived information that can live in search indexes. The distinction matters when a team is deciding what to change after a bad run. The trace shows what the agent actually did. Developers can use that evidence to revisit the context the application made available to the agent in the first place.

The appeal of putting search and observability on a common platform is easiest to see if you already use OpenSearch for one of them. Lewis describes teams starting with observability and then using the same technology to build a search application. They can draw on existing skills and reconsider how many places they keep copies of the same business data. 

Lardinois raises the issue of data gravity, and Lewis argues that the cost of changing platforms belongs in the total cost of ownership conversation alongside the bill for running them.

Who builds the next version?

Consolidation still takes time. Teams have applications in production for years, contracts that haven’t expired yet, and skills they’ll need to develop. Lewis and Lardinois discuss how a commercial ecosystem gives teams options for hosting and support along the way, and how an open project gives them a say in the features they’ll depend on.

“I think that contribution into OpenSearch can take many forms,” Lewis said. She points to pull requests, community Slack discussions, and user groups as ways to get involved. For early-career developers, she sees a chance to build a public record of how they work on a real system.

For experienced engineers, the systems thinking they bring to a production incident is especially valuable when an agent’s confident answer is the first clue something went sideways.

Lewis has a name for this shift. “I always joke — and I can say this because of my age — is that it’s sort of like revenge of the dinosaurs. We have now come to the stage where the person who understands the system-level context of what you’re trying to achieve with agentic AI becomes extremely important.”

Watch the full interview on The New Stack’s YouTube channel for more on what teams are building with OpenSearch, what the community is prioritizing, and how Lewis thinks about keeping control of your data as agent workloads grow.

AI agents can call the wrong API and still look healthy. OpenSearch’s Bianca Lewis explains how traces and cost data expose where a run went wrong.

item.title: Your AI agent’s “memory problem” may be something else
item.dc:creator: Daniela Pavlenco
item.description:
An agent may need additional context to continue when a user returns the next day. A workflow may resume from

The post Your AI agent’s “memory problem” may be something else appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
An agent may need additional context to continue when a user returns the next day. A workflow may resume from the wrong step, or a preference may be remembered without its scope, or a retrieval may return an outdated document. 

These are often described as “memory problems,” but they have different causes. Long-running agents rely on three kinds of context: workflow state to resume execution, durable information to carry across sessions, and external knowledge for the current request. Each needs a clear owner, lifecycle, and access boundary.

LangGraph and LangChain give developers useful abstractions, but the application still needs to define ownership, lifecycle, and access boundaries for each context type. Keeping those responsibilities explicit makes failures easier to diagnose and long-running agents easier to operate. 

A checkpoint can resume a workflow, but it cannot define memory

A workflow checkpoint answers a narrow question: Where should this run continue? 

In LangGraph, a checkpointer can persist graph state under a thread identifier so a workflow can pause for approval, recover after a process restart, or resume after a tool failure. That state can include messages, tool results, and execution progress. It supports durable execution, but persistence alone does not determine what an agent should remember across sessions. 

Consider a customer-support agent handling a subscription change. Its checkpoint stores the state needed to resume the workflow. If the customer expresses a preference, application rules determine whether to save it as a durable memory, and which customer or account it applies to. Retrieval supplies the current policy passage, filtered for the caller’s access. Each layer serves a different purpose and follows its own update rules.

“The layers can share a database without sharing a lifecycle. Make those distinctions in the data model so retaining workflow history doesn’t turn into agent memory.”

The layers can share a database without sharing a lifecycle. A checkpoint may expire with a run, a memory may remain until corrected or removed, and a knowledge record may change with its source. Make those distinctions in the data model so retaining workflow history doesn’t turn into agent memory. 

Give agent memory a lifecycle

Durable memory is information the application selects to carry across sessions. It must be possible to retrieve, validate, update, supersede, or delete. Each record should identify its owner, scope, source, and validity. 

A conversation can produce a candidate fact, but it becomes durable memory only after application rules or explicit user confirmation accepts it. When a fact changes, the earlier value is superseded. When deletion is requested, apply the defined scope to the source record and any derived memories or searchable data. Where retention rules permit, superseded records may remain as history but should be excluded from retrieval for current facts. 

“Scope, retention, correction, and deletion belong in the application and data model because a prompt that assembles the next context window cannot enforce those rules on its own.”

The lifecycle also includes boundaries. A preference for one user is not a global instruction. A tool outcome from one tenant should not become searchable context for another. Memory extracted from an untrusted document should not silently become policy. Scope, retention, correction, and deletion belong in the application and data model because a prompt that assembles the next context window cannot enforce those rules on its own.

RAG supplies knowledge for the current request

Retrieval-augmented generation brings relevant external knowledge into the current request. That knowledge may come from product documentation, support cases, or policy records. Retrieval can use keyword search for an exact identifier, vector search for a paraphrased request, SQL for current structured facts, or a hybrid route when measurement shows that combining signals helps.

Vector search ranks records by the distance or similarity between query and stored embeddings. That ranking is useful, but it doesn’t prove a record is current, authoritative, complete, or permitted for the caller. The retrieval path still needs source identifiers, versions, effective dates, metadata filters, tenant scope, and lifecycle rules. A semantically similar paragraph from an expired policy is still the wrong evidence.

RAG should not replace agent memory. A support manual is external knowledge, a workflow decision is application state, and a user preference may be durable memory. All can be searched with vectors, but their owners, access scopes, and update rules differ. 

Define the roles of LangGraph and LangChain

Frameworks make the application easier to compose, but they do not remove the need for boundaries. LangGraph is useful for representing a stateful workflow with nodes, transitions, checkpoints, and human approval points. LangChain provides abstractions for models, retrievers, tools, document processing, and application-side orchestration. Both can participate in a durable agent, but neither should be treated as the system of record for business data or as the final permission boundary.

“Frameworks make the application easier to compose, but they do not remove the need for boundaries. Clear ownership determines where to investigate a failure and which layer should enforce the fix.”

That division also makes troubleshooting more straightforward. If a workflow resumed from the wrong node, inspect the checkpoint. If the agent recalled an obsolete preference, inspect the memory lifecycle and its validity metadata. If the answer cited the wrong manual, inspect the retrieval query, source version, and filters. Frameworks provide the building blocks. Clear ownership determines where to investigate a failure and which layer should enforce the fix.

Design recovery alongside the primary workflow

An agent’s first demonstration usually follows the successful path: the model receives context, calls a tool, and returns an answer. A durable design also defines what happens when execution is interrupted, context conflicts, or evidence is missing. 

  • If a tool fails after a checkpoint, can the workflow resume without repeating a non-idempotent action?
  • If a memory changes, can the application identify the older record and mark it as superseded?
  • If a document is deleted or a tenant boundary changes, will retrieval exclude it before the model sees it?
  • If the required evidence is missing, does the agent ask for clarification or state that it cannot verify the answer?
  • If the final answer is wrong, can the team tell whether the failure came from checkpoint state, memory selection, retrieval, context assembly, or generation?

These questions determine what to trace: workflow identifiers, selected memory and source records, versions, scopes, retrieval routes, tool calls, permissions, and responses. Evidence should show how the system produced a response. 

Start with the boundaries, not the vector store

A practical starting point is small. Choose one workflow that needs to survive a restart or continue across sessions. Define the state required to resume it. Define the few facts that should become durable memory. Identify the external documents or records that belong in RAG, including their source and scope. Then test the three paths independently before combining them in the agent loop.

Choose retrieval methods to fit the information. Use structured queries for structured facts. Use vector or hybrid search when the question depends on meaning, wording, or related passages. Add memory promotion only when the application has a clear reason to retain something. Keep a correction and deletion path from the beginning so retained information stays accurate and useful as the system grows. 

An operable system should make three questions easy to answer: 

  1. Where did the workflow stop? 
  2. What does the application remember? 
  3. Which external evidence supports this response? 

LangGraph and LangChain can help implement the paths. A database with appropriate data access controls can store and retrieve related records, while the application manages their distinct lifecycles and access requirements. 

To try this architecture with Oracle AI Database Free, start with one workflow and test its checkpoint, memory, and retrieval paths independently. Use the Oracle AI Developer Hub for examples to adapt and the LangGraph and LangChain integrations documentation for implementation guidance.

The post Your AI agent’s “memory problem” may be something else appeared first on The New Stack.
Fix AI agent context failures by separating workflow checkpoints, durable memory, and RAG knowledge with clear ownership and lifecycles.

item.title: Anthropic says Claude writes and reviews 90% of its team’s code. The catch is how it checks the work.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Anthropic says Claude writes and reviews roughly 90% of the code produced by the team building Claude Code, and the

The post Anthropic says Claude writes and reviews 90% of its team’s code. The catch is how it checks the work. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic says Claude writes and reviews roughly 90% of the code produced by the team building Claude Code, and the company has spelled out how it verifies that work without making engineers inspect every change.

In a Monday engineering post, Anthropic technical staff member Addy Osmani describes a verification system built to support dozens or even hundreds of concurrent agents, where automated checks supply the evidence engineers need to judge what those agents produce.

The approach has attracted scrutiny from developers, much of it centered on the cost of model-driven verification and whether cheaper deterministic tooling could shoulder some of that load instead.

In response to questions from The New Stack, Anthropic walked through how it controls inference costs, stops agents from manipulating tests, and gauges whether its automated reviewers actually work.

Testing AI code live

The company has Claude exercise its changes inside a running application, leaning on browser automation for web apps, MCP-connected simulators for mobile builds, and local services for backend work.

Those instructions live in repository-specific verification skills under .claude/skills/, so an agent can run and check its own changes before it ever commits them.

Osmani also points developers toward property-based testing to flush out edge cases, along with differential testing to surface unanticipated behavior changes between an old implementation and a new one.

Keeping verification costs down

Not everyone is convinced the math works. Some developers questioned whether the extra inference costs were justified, and Hacker News commenter OtherShrezzing argues that reusable Playwright tests could handle much of the verification without repeatedly calling a model.

Anthropic tells The New Stack that inference costs swing considerably from one change to the next, and that it keeps them down by running the cheap, deterministic checks before any model gets involved.

“Deterministic checks like the build, linters, unit tests and property tests go first, because once Claude writes them they run as ordinary software and cost very little to rerun,” Anthropic tells The New Stack.

“Model review is for what a test can’t answer, like whether a change takes the right approach or misses a case nobody wrote a test for.”

“Model review is for what a test can’t answer, like whether a change takes the right approach or misses a case nobody wrote a test for.”

Anthropic would not put a specific figure on the added inference cost of model-based verification.

Stopping agents gaming tests

Hacker News user xnorswap raised a different worry: agents quietly reshaping code to get a failing test to pass.

“It’s not the per-run costs I worry about, it’s the costs of churn,” xnorswap writes, warning that an agent might rewrite the test or bolt on a workaround instead of fixing the underlying problem.

Anthropic has set rules for how Claude handles failing tests and, just as important, which parts of the repository its reviewer can trust.

“Our rule is that if a change can modify the check that judges it, the check is broken.”

“Our rule is that if a change can modify the check that judges it, the check is broken,” Anthropic tells The New Stack.

In practice, Code Review reads REVIEW.md from the base branch rather than from the changes introduced in a pull request, and any review result counts only for the exact commit it examined.

Claude is barred from skipping flaky tests, slipping in sleeps, or rerunning a test until it passes; when the agent can’t pin down the root cause, it deletes the test outright and documents why.

The team also logs how each commit was verified, including the cases where no verification happened at all.

Turning old bugs into guardrails

Of the 39 reliability checks the Claude Code team has accumulated, Claude typically runs only three to ten per change. For changes to session storage, for example, Claude checks whether older transcripts still load with –resume.

Commit gates require developers to verify changes through /code-review or /verify. Teams can monitor compliance before making the checks mandatory, and developers can bypass a gate if they explain why.

Anthropic tells The New Stack that between June and September, the number of merged pull requests to Claude Code’s codebase more than doubled, while the proportion of changes that had to be reverted fell by more than 40%.

The company did not say how much of that improvement came from its verification loops or provide separate figures for production defects and regressions.

Grading the code reviewers

To check its own reviewers, Anthropic grades them against historical incidents and reverts, recreating the repository as it existed at the moment of review and writing a one-sentence answer key for each case, with a reviewer earning credit only when its finding actually describes the bug in question.

Previously merged changes that stayed stable act as controls for catching false positives, and the company keeps a fixed test set walled off from the examples it uses to tune the reviewers.

Anthropic measures recall at several stages of the review pipeline, and even a reviewer that catches a genuine bug is scored as a miss if the finding never reaches an engineer.

The company says it does not currently publish the false-positive or false-negative rates from those Code Review evaluations.

Where engineers still earn their keep

Anthropic’s approach offers a framework for deciding which checks require model inference, and which deterministic tools can handle more cheaply. Without published reviewer error rates or detailed inference costs, however, developers have little data against which to benchmark their own implementations.

“A person is accountable for every change that ships, whoever typed it”

“A person is accountable for every change that ships, whoever typed it,” Anthropic tells The New Stack.

Engineers review the verification evidence, including test results and screenshots. If a check still fails after three rounds, Claude hands the problem to an engineer.

item.title: Does your AI agent need an LLM to decide what to do next?
item.dc:creator: Chris J. Preimesberger
item.description:
Say “good morning” to an AI agent, and it might search its long-term memory before saying hello back. Somewhere in

The post Does your AI agent need an LLM to decide what to do next? appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Say “good morning” to an AI agent, and it might search its long-term memory before saying hello back. Somewhere in that system, a service performs a semantic lookup to determine whether your greeting requires understanding your beverage preferences. Even if you take your coffee very seriously, this seems like a lot of infrastructure for two words.

Does this request need a more capable model than conventional options? Is this retrieved memory relevant? Should the workflow pause for a human?

This inefficiency and indecision is where Mike Chambers, a senior AI DevEx engineer at AWS, sees an opportunity. In a conversation last month at AGNTCon + MCPCon North America 2026 in San Jose, California, Chambers explained to The New Stack Editor-in-Chief Nick Lucchesi how developers can use decider models to handle the small judgments that add up inside an agent. 

Decider models (also called decision models or System One models) are specialized AI models that choose from a fixed set of options or rate inputs on a scale — returning calibrated probabilities without generating free-form text. Popularized by TypeSafe AI’s Jev, they give software and agentic workflows fast, low-latency judgments with explicit confidence scores. (AWS’s Strands Labs released its own open-source decision model, the 2-billion-parameter Strands Decider 2B, on October 1.)

An if statement with a feel for language

Chambers describes the approach as “a little bit like having an agentic-powered ‘if’ statement inside of your code.”

Developers have used classifiers for years. What makes this generation of decider models interesting, Chambers told The New Stack, is that general-purpose pretraining lets you try one on a new classification task without first training a model of your own. You supply context in natural language, ask a question about it, and get a numeric score your application can use to choose a branch.

In the models Chambers describes, that score comes back in a single forward pass. There’s no token sequence to generate. That can make a decider attractive for a choice that sits on the critical path of every request. A model router, for example, can use a score to send routine prompts to a smaller model and reserve a more capable one for harder jobs. The potential savings come from both the routing decision itself and the downstream work it saves.

When an agent can skip the memory search

Chambers tried the idea with the open-source Strands framework and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Memory. He put Strands Decider in front of the memory lookup to judge whether an incoming message called for fetching anything from past conversations. A greeting could go straight through. A request that depends on something the user said earlier could still trigger a search.

He also tried using a decider after retrieval. A memory service can return the top matches to a query, but some may have little bearing on the task at hand. A decider can score each result for relevance before the agent includes it in the context it sends to the model. One decision can save a service call. The other can give the model less extraneous material to sort through.

A predictable output still needs testing

A number in a predictable JSON field makes a decider easy to wire into an application. Whether that number is reliable enough to act on takes testing. “Will the number be correct? That’s for your testing to be able to go and figure out whether that’s the case or not,” Chambers said.

Chambers calls his memory experiment experimental. The interview also gets into what happens when the stakes rise. A missed preference might mean a mediocre coffee recommendation. An agent about to spend money is a different matter, and Chambers argues for checks outside the agent’s loop and human approval for decisions that are hard to reverse.

Watch the full interview on The New Stack’s YouTube channel for Chambers’ walkthrough of the memory experiment and a look at where developers are taking open-source deciders next, from documents to robotics.

Every agent makes small judgment calls. AWS’s Mike Chambers says decider models can make them in one pass, with a confidence score your code can use.

item.title: Google just gave Gemini the run of your Mac — three days after Apple tightened the rules
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Google is adding computer use to its Gemini app for macOS. The assistant can now work across desktop applications and

The post Google just gave Gemini the run of your Mac — three days after Apple tightened the rules appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Google is adding computer use to its Gemini app for macOS. The assistant can now work across desktop applications and websites in a separate background window without taking over the user’s screen. Gemini handles tasks in the background while users continue working.

The feature includes a live preview in the chat so users can monitor the agent’s activity, pause execution, and approve actions when necessary.

The company’s announcement Thursday comes just three days after Apple introduced tighter permission controls for macOS automation.

The company’s announcement Thursday comes just three days after Apple introduced tighter permission controls for macOS automation. Google hasn’t explained how Gemini will operate under the new restrictions.

Apple tightens agent permissions

The macOS 27.3 beta 2 changes split Device Control and Data Access permissions into two categories; System & App Protection Override and Accessibility.

Apps requesting broad system access will face more explicit permission prompts, and users can approve individual requests instead of granting ongoing access.

Developers building desktop agents will also need to account for least-privilege access, since users can restrict or revoke permissions while an agent is running.

Gemini’s new Mac powers

Google says Gemini can extract shipping details from local PDFs, gather dashboard metrics for presentations, edit batches of photos, and work with 3D design software.

The company hasn’t detailed how the background environment is isolated from macOS, how it maintains state across applications, or which actions require user approval.

Google’s existing computer-use API

Google introduced computer use with Gemini 2.5 in October 2025 and later integrated it directly into Gemini 3.5 Flash.

According to the developer documentation, the model works from screenshots and returns actions for client-side execution. Developers manage the execution environment, while the API provides configurable safety policies, and optional screenshot scanning for prompt injection.

The new Mac feature is part of the consumer Gemini app, not a separate developer API.

The new Mac feature is part of the consumer Gemini app, not a separate developer API. It’s unclear whether the app uses the same execution architecture or whether Google plans to open its background environment to third-party developers.

Where Google stays silent

The company has documented prompt-injection safeguards for its developer-facing computer-use tools but hasn’t said which protections are built into the Mac app. Agents with access to local files and privileged applications also risk untrusted input reaching the agent harness, and influencing the actions it executes.

Reliability questions remain unanswered since the company has not shared any performance figures for the Mac app or explained what happens when an action fails, or an application behaves unexpectedly.

Reliability questions remain unanswered since the company has not shared any performance figures for the Mac app or explained what happens when an action fails, or an application behaves unexpectedly.

Rollout, requirements and tiers

Gemini computer use is rolling out in English in the United States for personal Google accounts belonging to users 18 and older. The feature requires an Apple Silicon Mac running macOS Sequoia 15.0 or later and a Google AI Plus, Pro, or Ultra subscription.

item.title: An engineer didn’t message his AI for 22 of 44 days. It built an Android app anyway.
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Cognition has spent nearly three years developing Devin as an autonomous engineer that takes a ticket and ships a pull

The post An engineer didn’t message his AI for 22 of 44 days. It built an Android app anyway. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Cognition has spent nearly three years developing Devin as an autonomous engineer that takes a ticket and ships a pull request.

With Tuesday’s launch of Devin Bots, the company is moving into management, introducing persistent agents that oversee multiple Devin coding sessions, and take responsibility for engineering outcomes over days or weeks.

Coordination becomes the product

CEO Scott Wu argues that eliminating even a small amount of remaining human work could produce outsized productivity gains. In a post on X, he asks how much more developers could accomplish if coding agents went from handling 98% of their work to 99%, and says Cognition had seen enormous differences among beta testers and internal teams.

The percentages are hypothetical, but Wu is making the case that coordination, not just coding, is the next opportunity for automation.

The percentages are hypothetical, but Wu is making the case that coordination, not just coding, is the next opportunity for automation.

From tickets to targets

Cognition founding team member Silas Alberti described the change in a post on X as a move toward assigning agents ongoing goals instead of individual tasks. He says the team has already used Devin Bots to compress weeks of research into days.

The company shares the example of keeping an Android app in sync with its iOS version. As new features are added to iOS, a Devin Bot can assign the corresponding Android work without an engineer having to create a ticket for every update.

The idea builds on a trend toward coding agents that function as team members. Devin Bots takes that a step further by putting an agent in charge of coordinating the work.

An Android app, barely supervised

When the company set out to build an Android version of Devin, it had no dedicated Android engineers. Instead, the company assigned the project to a Devin Bot on September 28 and let it coordinate the coding work.

Over the next 44 days, Cognition says the Bot merged 1,134 pull requests, wrote 344,651 lines of Kotlin and closed 1,217 tickets. It also ran 2,841 screenshot tests. The engineer overseeing the project sent 183 messages during that period, including none on 22 of those days.

In its write-up, Cognition explains that the Bot opened tickets and assigned them to individual Devin sessions, then merged changes once they passed continuous integration and Devin Review. The team could follow along through daily Slack updates that included screen recordings. The Android app is now in open testing on Google Play, though it still needs work before it matches the iOS version.

Cognition’s Layout Bot checks the company’s web app for visual bugs every three hours, rebuilds the latest production code, and tests the interface under different loading conditions. Engineers merged 159 of its fixes over three weeks, reducing layout lag by 70%, according to Cognition.

Cognition says the studio went from producing around 50 pull requests a week to 1,900.

A mobile game studio also has roughly 20 bots reporting to another agent named Super Jenny. Four times a day, Super Jenny brings decisions to a human operator. Cognition says the studio went from producing around 50 pull requests a week to 1,900.

Where oversight runs thin

Multiple coding agents working on the same project can introduce conflicting dependencies or bugs that affect other agents’ work. Cognition hasn’t explained how Devin Bots handle those conflicts.

Tasks requiring approval go to a “Needs You” inbox for an engineer to review.

Developers can protect specific CI checks and set compute spending limits before assigning a project to a Bot. Tasks requiring approval go to a “Needs You” inbox for an engineer to review. The company hasn’t disclosed how the supervising Bot decides when code is ready to merge or when repeated failures warrant human intervention.

Code verification remains another concern when agents write tests for their own implementations. Agent-generated pull requests are already putting pressure on conventional code review pipelines, and some teams are developing independent verification loops to catch errors that the original coding agent might miss.

The New Stack has asked Cognition for more information about how Devin Bots coordinate parallel agents, evaluate completed work and determine when human intervention is necessary.

Cognition hasn’t disclosed how much engineering time was spent reviewing the Bots’ pull requests or fixing failed implementations.

Cognition’s Devin Bots put AI agents in charge of teams of Devin coding agents, running software projects for weeks with little human direction.

item.title: “Be ready for change”: AAIF’s CTO on why the agent stack won’t settle
item.dc:creator: Chris J. Preimesberger
item.description:
If you’ve spent any time over the past year trying to get AI agents to talk to each other without

The post “Be ready for change”: AAIF’s CTO on why the agent stack won’t settle appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
If you’ve spent any time over the past year trying to get AI agents to talk to each other without tearing your architecture apart, you know the struggle: vendor lock-in, fragmented protocols, and context that definitely vanishes the second you attempt to make a cross-framework handoff.

It’s astounding how fast developers’ needs have changed just in 10 months since the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) was formed to help solve those problems. 

The Linux Foundation-backed AAIF gives shared agent infrastructure a home outside any one vendor’s control. It launched in December 2025 with three projects, including the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which connects AI applications to external tools and data.

On October 22, Anthropic contributed Agent Skills, and OpenAI contributed Open Responses to the foundation, alongside projects from Hugging Face and Alibaba. The additions brought AAIF to 10 hosted projects.

The New Stack Editor-in-Chief Nick Lucchesi sat down with Manik Surtani, AAIF’s co-founder and CTO, for The New Stack podcast at AGNTCon + MCPCon in San Jose, shortly after Surtani announced the additions in his October 22 keynote. The news was still fresh — the problems behind it, though, were all too familiar.

“I think that’s always been there,” Surtani said of the needs these projects address. “We’ve always known that sandboxes are really important.” Agent Skills, too, was already in use before joining the foundation. What had changed was where these projects would be governed.

“…having a standardized way to speak to a model is super important.”

“I’m really happy [Agent Skills] is here. And Open Responses as well. I mean, having a standardized way to speak to a model is super important. And I’m glad to see that it’s now happening in a way that is vendor-neutral, in a neutral governance and everything else.”

Four giant projects join the foundation

The big news from Surtani was this: Four heavy-hitting projects had joined the AAIF. Here’s what each brings to the table:

  • Agent Skills (Anthropic): An open format for bundling instructions, scripts, and reference materials that an agent can load when it needs to perform a particular task. Write those instructions once, and use them across agents that support the format.
  • Open Responses (OpenAI): An open specification, based on OpenAI’s Responses API, for how applications send requests to language models and receive results. A shared format means less translation work when developers switch between compatible model providers.
  • OpenEnv (Hugging Face): A framework for building and sharing reinforcement learning environments, where agents practice tasks and receive feedback that can be used to train them.
  • OpenSandbox (Alibaba): A platform for running agent-generated code and other work in isolated environments, separating that execution from the surrounding system.

While Anthropic, OpenAI, Hugging Face, and Alibaba rallying around a neutral foundation sounds like an AI miracle, Surtani noted that developer demand for open governance has existed from Day 1.

“More than faster, I think people are going to be able to build on top of things that they can trust more.”

“More than faster, I think people are going to be able to build on top of things that they can trust more,” Surtani said. “It’s not like you couldn’t trust open responses before. Of course you could. But now everyone has a say in how it’s going to grow and how it’s going to get shaped.”

Developers learned this lesson the hard way during the early cloud-native boom. Nobody wants to build core enterprise infrastructure on tech they can’t help steer.

Tackling the real pain points: Agent memory and portability

What problem keeps Surtani up at night? In the near term, it’s agent memory and context management — the information an agent needs to keep working on a task, including what’s already happened. A harness is the software around a model that manages its tools and workflow. Carrying that context from one model or harness to another remains difficult, Surtani said; he wants teams to be able to share it across the agents and people working on the same problem.

Beyond context portability, Surtani emphasized that software engineering teams should design for model independence right now using abstractions, proxies, and standardized interfaces. In practical terms, that means keeping the application from being tied too tightly to one model provider: A proxy or router sits between the application and the model, letting a team switch the model behind the scenes. It doesn’t solve everything, he cautioned, but it handles much of the heavy lifting.

Unlike the cloud stack associated with the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) — which Surtani described as already well-defined — the agentic AI stack is inherently fluid.

“My advice to people is just be ready for change. Change is going to happen.”

“My advice to people is just be ready for change. Change is going to happen,” Surtani told The New Stack. “Now, the good thing in all of this is that change is actually easy as well. With agents actually building themselves and writing code, it’s not going to be that expensive or that hard to migrate from one thing to the other.”

A sandbox for early-stage projects

With more than 300 member organizations signing on in just 10 months (ranging from fintechs to non-tech giants such as the Gates Foundation), AAIF realized its initial high barrier to entry — borrowed from the mature CNCF template — was ill-suited for a space evolving at warp speed.

To adapt, the foundation launched a new Sandbox lifecycle phase on September 1 to bring in early-stage, high-momentum community tools before they hit massive enterprise scale.

This Sandbox phase is a project maturity category, separate from the isolated execution environments provided by OpenSandbox. It gives promising young projects a place to develop under neutral governance, even before they have widespread production use.

Surtani’s main call-to-action for developers? Push your vendors for open standards, transparent specs, and true longevity.

Watch the full interview

Watch our full interview with Surtani to get his take on agentic commerce, agent permissions, advertising without human eyes, and why an AI stack might never fully solidify. Subscribe to The New Stack‘s YouTube channel to keep up with our new episodes as they are released.
