Anthropic and OpenAI handed their agent specs to a neutral foundation. AAIF’s CTO explains what that changes and what developers should build for next.

item.title: IDrive wants to back up your coding agents, too
item.dc:creator: Frederic Lardinois
item.description:
Coding agents need backups, too, or at least that’s what IDrive is arguing. Backup and storage service IDrive on Thursday

The post IDrive wants to back up your coding agents, too appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Coding agents need backups, too, or at least that’s what IDrive is arguing.

Backup and storage service IDrive on Thursday announced AI Agents Backup, a feature in its desktop app that finds the data these agents store locally for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and Cline and copies it to the user’s IDrive account.

By default, agents tend to keep a lot of their state on a developer’s machine, including session transcripts, instruction files, and MCP server configurations. The problem is that most of this sits in hidden folders that developers rarely look at.

Thing is, some of this data is actually valuable. A session transcript, after all, is a record of how a developer and an agent got to a fix, and this local data also helps agents like Claude Code and Codex pick up from old sessions to continue a task days later. Then, there are the AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md files and things like MCP configurations that involve some setup work that few developers will want to have to redo when something goes awry.

As IDrive CEO Raghu Kulkarni notes in the announcement, “Most of that data lives only on the local machine and has been left out of backup plans.” The history and configuration these agents build up, he says, is “a real work product.”

Session history is easily lost

Some of this data is also easy to lose. By default, Claude Code deletes session transcripts older than 30 days. Users have actually filed a long list of GitHub issues about history that disappeared without warning and Cursor’s forum has plenty of threads from users whose chat history disappeared after an update.

What IDrive backs up

For Claude, the new backup feature covers Claude Code history from both the terminal and the desktop app, plus settings, instruction files, and local MCP server configurations. It also picks up Cowork scheduled tasks that Team and Enterprise users chose to keep on their own machine.

The Cursor backup includes chat history, workspace data, keybindings, extensions, and the Cursor Agent CLI’s sessions. Codex and Cline get similar treatment.

It’s worth noting that IDrive skips caches and temporary files. It also doesn’t back up source code and repositories, because the company expects users to protect them with its regular file backup. Any chats that live on a provider’s servers are also out of bounds.

When a user wants to restore these files, IDrive puts them back into their original location. One thing to note is that, for Claude, IDrive’s documentation says it replaces whatever is there. Restoring also only works between machines that run the same operating system, which means a Windows setup can’t be restored to a Mac, for example.

Open source backup alternatives

This idea, of course, isn’t entirely new. Developers can already use a plethora of open source tools to sync and back up their agent’s state.

There are tools like bak, which syncs agent configurations, and commercial services like Agent Bak. Agent-archive, meanwhile, ships session transcripts to an S3 or R2 bucket and backup specialist Backblaze’s labs team has published an open source engine for backing up agent state to its B2 storage service.

IDrive’s version is built into a consumer backup app and can automatically detect the four agents on its own. It also comes with a restore flow that is meant for moving to a new computer.

AI Agents Backup is available now in the IDrive desktop app for all users, the company says. Gemini CLI, GitHub Copilot, and Windsurf aren’t on the supported list.

IDrive’s new AI Agents Backup protects the session history and configs that Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, and Cline keep on a developer’s machine.

item.title: A “headless Slack”: Vercel’s new message board lets Claude Code and Codex agents work together
item.dc:creator: Paul Sawers
item.description:
For AI agents to work together effectively, they need a way to communicate and divvy up tasks — much as

The post A “headless Slack”: Vercel’s new message board lets Claude Code and Codex agents work together appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
For AI agents to work together effectively, they need a way to communicate and divvy up tasks — much as humans already do through a swath of digital collaboration tools.

Vercel is tackling this with Board, an experimental shared message board through which agents can claim tasks, exchange findings and track progress across different tools and environments, while allowing developers to follow and intervene in the work.

In a blog post published on Wednesday, Vercel says it developed Board for its own engineering operations, first using it to coordinate security agents investigating vulnerabilities and submitting fixes. It then rebuilt v0’s software factory around Board, which Vercel says now “merges over 50% of PRs.”

“It packages what we’ve learned about coordinating work across agent fleets.”

“It packages what we’ve learned about coordinating work across agent fleets and builds towards a future where multiple teams of humans and agents orchestrate swarms, software factories, and other agentic workflows,” the company writes.

The coordination conundrum

OpenAI demonstrated the importance of multi-agent communication in September when it announced that its agents had solved the Navier–Stokes problem, a longstanding mathematical challenge concerning the behavior of fluids.

The company said some 10,000 agents operated concurrently in the group that produced the result, exchanging information as they worked.

“In the process of resolving the Navier–Stokes problem, the agents sent 2.7 million messages and used approximately 130 billion output tokens,” the company wrote.

The need to manage multiple agents in parallel is becoming increasingly apparent in software development. Just last week, Google and Cursor introduced competing approaches to coordinating coding agents, with Google focusing on agents working on behalf of a single developer and Cursor enabling agents belonging to different teammates to communicate.

Then on Tuesday, Replit introduced Missions, bringing multiple agents together to tackle larger development projects.

Elsewhere, companies are also turning to existing collaboration platforms to bring humans and AI agents together. Devin Bots, which Cognition launched on Tuesday, uses Slack to connect agents with their human teammates.

In an X post published on Thursday, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff says more than 226,000 custom agents have been deployed to Slack from across the major agent-building platforms. Notably, he says that he hadn’t anticipated this use of Slack when Salesforce acquired it back in 2021, acknowledging that companies are now using the platform as “trusted agent infrastructure.”

Vercel itself added its Agent to Slack code channels in August, allowing teammates to follow its work, give instructions and review proposed changes.

With Board, Vercel provides channels and threaded discussions where agents can pick up assignments, exchange findings, monitor dependencies and record completed work. It also maintains a history of activity, allowing developers to follow what their agents have been doing.

Crucially, Board is designed to accommodate agents built on different technologies. Vercel explicitly lists Claude Code, Codex, Pi, OpenCode, eve, fx, Mastra and LangChain, as tools that can work together through Board.

“This is an important building block for software factories, self-optimizing systems, and scientific research.”

In an X post published on Wednesday, Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch described the technology as a “message board infrastructure primitive.” Or, a “headless Slack” for agents.

“This is an important building block for software factories, self-optimizing systems, and scientific research, where the human prompting is just the seed of the system, and millions of agents can operate in a decentralized fashion,” Rauch writes, adding that Board is designed to work independently of any particular model, agent harness or hosting provider.

“Just bring your agents, give them our CLI, and watch magic happen,” he adds.

Keeping humans in the loop

Board also connects agents to the tools developers already use, including Slack, GitHub and Linear. For example, a developer can submit a request through Slack, which an agent can then pick up and break into smaller assignments for other agents to complete.

The ensuing discussion, task ownership and progress updates are maintained in Board.

As work progresses, Board can synchronize information with GitHub, allowing agents and developers to follow changes to pull requests and review feedback, without having to manually relay information between systems. It also supports event-driven triggers, so agents can resume work when new messages arrive or task statuses change.

It’s worth noting that human oversight remains a crucial part of the process. Agents can report findings and wait for developers to approve changes before proceeding, while Board also provides channel-level permissions that determine which people and agents can access information or perform particular actions.

The security question

The ability of agents to communicate independently raises key questions about who controls those conversations and what information they can exchange.

Indeed, Rauch points to the OpenAI/Hugging Face cybersecurity incident from July as another high-profile example of message boards facilitating agent coordination. During the breach, agents repurposed an internal software repository to exchange findings and coordinate their activities.

“A core part of why we built Vercel Board was to fulfill our own needs for security and auditability.”

Thus, security and oversight are key considerations for systems such as Board. Vercel says it built access controls and activity logs into the service, allowing teams to restrict which agents can interact with particular channels and track their actions.

“A core part of why we built Vercel Board was to fulfill our own needs for security and auditability,” the company writes.

The accompanying documentation also warns that agents may “read messages as instructions,” making it important to control who can post in channels where agents receive tasks. By default, channels are accessible to team members, project deployments and installed apps unless administrators restrict access. Vercel recommends creating private channels or restricting permissions where necessary, and keeping sensitive information such as API keys and tokens off Board entirely.

Vercel Board is available now as an experimental feature on all Vercel plans, accessible through the Vercel CLI or JavaScript SDK. It’s free during the experimental period, though Vercel says it may introduce charges later.

The post A “headless Slack”: Vercel’s new message board lets Claude Code and Codex agents work together appeared first on The New Stack.
Vercel Board lets agents divvy up work, share findings, and sync with Slack and GitHub. It follows swarm launches from Cursor, Google, and Replit.

item.title: Where should AI workloads run? Probably next to the data.
item.dc:creator: Shubham Thakur
item.description:
AWS raised prices on EC2 Capacity Blocks, its reserved GPU capacity, by about 15% in January and about 20% in

The post Where should AI workloads run? Probably next to the data. appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
AWS raised prices on EC2 Capacity Blocks, its reserved GPU capacity, by about 15% in January and about 20% in July. Picture a platform team watching a training job’s bill climb after copying a few hundred terabytes of sensor data across regions just to reach the GPUs, then realizing the data never had to move.

For AI workloads, the real question is whether the workload goes to the data or the data goes to the workload. Data gravity usually answers it.

Data gravity hits AI workloads harder than it ever hit analytics

Data gravity is the tendency of compute, applications, and services to be pulled toward large concentrations of data, because moving the data costs more than moving the logic that processes it. The larger a dataset grows, the more expensive every copy becomes, and the more everything that needs that data ends up living next to it.

Scheduled BI often tolerates periodic queries against sampled or aggregated data. Large training runs can require repeated reads of a much larger dataset, while agents retrieve fresh context throughout a workflow. When those reads cross regions or environments, transfer costs and latency add up. Each agent output also becomes new data that feeds the next round of retrieval, which compounds the pull over time.

A January 2026 analysis in BigDATAwire argued that AI workloads removed the cushion that let enterprises leave data gravity unmanaged for a decade. The year’s pricing moves make the same point from the cost side. Combined, the two increases add up to roughly 38% on the H200 instances that took both.

Moving data to the compute stops working at AI scale

Centralizing compute can require copying data into its environment before a job starts, and that transfer may carry charges.

For illustration, assume a transfer rate of $0.02 per GB and a 300 TB dataset (300,000 GB). The transfer alone would cost $6,000 per copy. That’s a hypothetical, not an AWS quote. Real charges depend on source, destination, route, service, and terms, so cross-region and cloud-to-premises movement needs explicit costing. Remote reads also add network latency, which matters when a workload has a tight response-time target.

“Transfer bills, duplicate pipelines and the engineering hours spent maintaining them belong in the placement calculation alongside compute charges.”

Two more costs rarely show up next to the GPU rate:

  • Interoperability overhead: cross-environment pipelines need their own translation layers when engines, query languages, connectors, and software development kits (SDKs) differ.
  • Lock-in: transfer charges and the engineering work of moving data and pipelines can make leaving an environment expensive.

Transfer bills, duplicate pipelines and the engineering hours spent maintaining them belong in the placement calculation alongside compute charges.

Moving compute to the data instead

A scheduling and placement layer can send a job to an environment that already holds its data, avoiding repeated full-dataset transfers. The job still needs compatible accelerators, enough memory, a supported runtime, and adequate storage throughput. Model weights, container images and checkpoints may also need to move.

Making that decision well means evaluating four inputs together, every time a job is scheduled:

A placement layer first excludes environments that violate residency or access rules, then compares feasible options by capacity, performance, and total cost. It dispatches the job with its runtime policies and revisits placement when those conditions change.

Where a specific workload belongs depends on the workload

There’s no universal rule. It’s a workload-by-workload decision.

Bursty training: public cloud can suit elastic demand, provided suitable GPU capacity is available, and transfer costs don’t erase the benefit.

Residency-restricted work: applicable law or contract determines the permitted jurisdiction and environment. An approved in-region cloud can qualify where an out-of-region on-premises cluster cannot. Large data volume adds an economic constraint, not a legal one.

Transaction-near inference: place execution close enough to the transaction to meet its latency target, whether in cloud, on-premises or at the edge.

Back to the platform team. Their training job reads a large dataset from an on-premises store, and policy excludes processing outside an approved region. A local cluster has the required GPU memory and runtime. An approved cloud region offers suitable GPUs but requires copying the dataset. So they compare completion time and total cost, including transfer, storage, and queueing. If local execution meets the deadline at lower total cost, the job runs there with the same access controls. If not, they assess the approved cloud option.

If neither environment meets policy and capacity requirements, the job is queued or rejected rather than sent to an unapproved region with restricted data. They record the choice and its assumptions so a price change, a growing dataset, or a missed deadline triggers a new review.

Formal policy on all this is uneven. In BARC’s State of Data and AI Governance study, which Acceldata sponsored, 56% of North American respondents report formal sovereignty policies for AI processing and storage, against 30% in Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA). That runs against expectations, since Europe is known for strict data rules. EMEA respondents also name siloed data as a top governance obstacle more than twice as often as their North American peers, 35% versus 17%.

Hybrid architecture matters more than picking a cloud

Hybrid can be a lasting architecture, not merely a stop on the way to the cloud. Data-heavy, latency-sensitive, or sovereignty-bound work can stay on-premises, while the cloud handles demand where elasticity is worth the cost.

It needs common operational controls across both environments: identity, runtime compatibility, observability, and policy enforcement. An all-cloud estate incurs transfer and lock-in costs when data must leave a region or provider. An all-on-premises estate leaves bursty work waiting for fixed capacity.

“Hybrid can be a lasting architecture, not merely a stop on the way to the cloud.”

Job portability helps only where the target environment supports the required engines, dependencies, and hardware. Open table formats such as Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, and Apache Hudi help here, because several engines can read the same tables in place. Moving the job doesn’t have to mean converting or copying the data first.

This is the problem Acceldata built its xLake platform around: keep data where it lives, in open formats, and bring governed compute to it across cloud and on-premises environments. 

Sovereign AI requires more than GPU power

The sovereign AI conversation usually starts with GPUs, but GPU compute alone is an incomplete architecture. Owning or reserving GPU capacity says nothing about whether the data feeding those GPUs, or the retrieval and orchestration layers around them, stays inside infrastructure the organization controls. Sovereignty is a property of the whole data and AI stack. Compute is one layer of it.

For a strict customer-controlled boundary, Acceldata’s May 2026 analysis of sovereign GPU infrastructure identifies four controls: 

  • Route tool calls through internally hosted endpoints so operational data, prompts, and workflow context never leave the organization’s network.
  • Retrieval infrastructure (embedding indexes and vector search) running on infrastructure the organization controls rather than a provider-managed vector service.
  • Orchestration of prompts, memory, and intermediate agent state inside the organization’s own environment.
  • Access policies for permissions and retrieval scope enforced within that same governed boundary.

“A workload can run on the most expensive reserved GPUs available and still fail a sovereignty review if its prompts, embeddings, or agent state cross a boundary they were never cleared to cross.”

Placement decisions inherit all four. A workload can run on the most expensive reserved GPUs available and still fail a sovereignty review if its prompts, embeddings, or agent state cross a boundary they were never cleared to cross.

The workload goes where the data already lives

Changes in compute prices are a reason to revisit placement, not proof that one environment is always cheaper. Transfer charges, storage, engineering effort, and completion time belong in the same comparison. That makes the cost of reaching the data a first-order input to any placement call, not a footnote to the GPU rate.

Keep the assumptions with each decision: dataset location, permitted destinations, compatible capacity, expected completion time, and total cost. When one changes, review the affected workload. Where running beside the data wins, move the job instead of the dataset.

Teams that revisit placement now, while their datasets are still manageable, will spend less fighting data gravity later than teams that keep copying data to wherever the GPUs happen to be.

That’s the lesson the platform team learned the hard way at the start of this piece. The data never had to move. The job did.

The post Where should AI workloads run? Probably next to the data. appeared first on The New Stack.
Data gravity and rising GPU costs make copying datasets unsustainable. Move AI workloads to your data with governed hybrid placement.

item.title: How Amazon ECS handles blue/green, canary, and linear deployments
item.dc:creator: Simon Gao
item.description:
Deploying containers safely at scale can mean assembling your own system: traffic-splitting logic, alarm evaluation, rollback automation, approval gates. It’s

The post How Amazon ECS handles blue/green, canary, and linear deployments appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Deploying containers safely at scale can mean assembling your own system: traffic-splitting logic, alarm evaluation, rollback automation, approval gates. It’s infrastructure that exists solely to protect the deployment itself. AWS has built all of those capabilities directly into Amazon Elastic Container Service (ECS), so you don’t have to.

“Deploying containers safely at scale can mean assembling your own system: traffic-splitting logic, alarm evaluation, rollback automation, approval gates. It’s infrastructure that exists solely to protect the deployment itself.”

You can access all these tools through a single API endpoint. AWS built them to work out of the box when you use Amazon ECS as your container orchestration platform with the Amazon ECS deployment controller. As a result, you don’t have to build your own abstractions or learn a new framework to get the deployment behavior you want. Instead, you pick and choose the features you want through a service deployment configuration and update it as your needs change.

How the building blocks map to ECS

If you’ve run progressive delivery on Kubernetes with Argo Rollouts or Flagger, you know the shape of the stack: a controller you install and keep current, analysis wired to your metrics backend, and a traffic provider for weighted canaries. Argo Rollouts approximates canary weights with replica counts and uses an ingress controller, service mesh, or Gateway API for precise percentages. Flagger uses a service mesh or ingress controller for weighted canaries, and plain Kubernetes Services for blue/green. Both are mature open-source projects and a great fit when you want to own and tune every layer. ECS takes a different approach and builds the same capabilities into the service. Here’s a comparison of the different deployment controllers:

When are rolling deployments not enough?

Rolling deployments are where ECS started, and they’re still the right default for most customers. In a rolling deployment, ECS replaces tasks running the old version with tasks running the new one, a batch at a time. New tasks start receiving production traffic as soon as they pass health checks, and ECS stops old tasks as the new ones take over. Two settings, minimumHealthyPercent and maximumPercent, control how many tasks can be replaced at once and how much extra capacity the deployment can use. Rolling deployments work with both the deployment circuit breaker and CloudWatch alarm-based automatic rollback, which we’ll cover below.

So, where’s the gap? Let’s say you have an API service running on ECS behind an ALB. You ship a large refactor. A bug surfaces, but it takes time because of metric emission and alarm-processing delays. By the time your alarm fires, a large share of your tasks (maybe all of them) are already running the new version and serving production traffic. ECS rolls back for you, but in a rolling deployment, rollback means another rollout of the previous task definition: ECS must launch new tasks, pass health checks, and replace the bad ones. Your application’s availability will be exposed for some time.

“There’s a limit to how fast a rolling deployment can roll back, which increases customer impact (measured by failed requests per unit of time) from the new, bad application version.”

So, there’s a limit to how fast a rolling deployment can roll back, which increases customer impact (measured by failed requests per unit of time) from the new, bad application version. Blue/green deployments can shorten the duration of the impact. With ECS’s built-in blue/green strategy, the old version stays running alongside the new one for a configurable bake period (up to 24 hours). All production traffic routes to the new version, but the old version’s tasks remain registered and ready to take traffic with a flip of a switch. If something goes wrong, rollback is a simple traffic shift, and not a complete redeploy.

The tradeoff is that you’re doubling compute capacity during the deployment window. For services where a bad release serving 100% of traffic for even a few minutes is costly, that tradeoff is worth it.

How does ECS know something went wrong?

How would Amazon ECS know when to flip traffic back? There are several ways to perform a service deployment rollback, and they’re all configurable through an ECS service’s deployment configuration:

  • Task launch and health state monitoring during a deployment through circuit breaker
  • Amazon CloudWatch alarm(s) monitoring and auto-rollback
  • Controls to roll back an ongoing service deployment through the StopServiceDeployment API
  • Service deployment lifecycle hooks (Lambda or pause target type)

For API server failures, you can set up Amazon CloudWatch alarms to monitor server response codes and trigger a rollback when a high volume of 4xx or 5xx codes is detected. But what if your application monitoring constructs are outside of Amazon CloudWatch and stored on another service like Datadog, Splunk, or Grafana? With service deployment lifecycle hooks, you can implement your own automation that polls these data sources for alarm data by implementing that logic in a Lambda function and configuring a Lambda target type. The primary consideration is configuring the lifecycle hook for the POST_PRODUCTION_TRAFFIC_SHIFT stage.

If you can’t use Lambda functions, then implement an Amazon EventBridge trigger with a pause hook target type instead. Amazon ECS will send an Amazon EventBridge event when the service deployment reaches the lifecycle stage configured for the lifecycle hook. The trigger should fire a process you own that runs the same polling loop to monitor an alarm or metric. Once the monitoring condition succeeds, call the ContinueServiceDeployment API to allow the service deployment to progress.

In addition to alarms and lifecycle hooks, the service deployment circuit breaker monitor can stop a bad deployment from progressing. This deployment monitor looks for failed or unhealthy tasks during a service deployment and compares the sum against a threshold. With configurable circuit breaker settings, you can customize the counter algorithm to ignore intermittent task launch or health failures. You can also customize the failure threshold based on your application’s needs.

Advanced deployment strategies

The example above is just one way to use built-in ECS features to customize your service deployment. If a one-step traffic shift isn’t suitable for your application, linear and canary deployments are also alternatives.

Linear and canary deployments are like blue/green deployments in that they use well-defined traffic-shift steps to isolate application traffic between versions. Linear deployments move traffic in equal increments based on your configuration. Canaries are a little different in that there is a two-step migration in application traffic as opposed to n number of incremental shifts.

Not advanced enough? There’s more!

All the deployment tools we talked about today apply to all deployment strategies that ECS supports. Similarly, all deployment strategies are compatible with ECS Service Connect and VPC Lattice network integrations. The only caveat is that lifecycle hooks can be applied to only two stages for a rolling deployment, since that lifecycle is inherently simpler than blue/green, linear, or canary deployments.

“All deployment strategies also work without a load balancer, ECS Service Connect, or VPC Lattice integration! That’s right, even blue/green, linear, and canary deployments.”

All deployment strategies also work without a load balancer, ECS Service Connect, or VPC Lattice integration! That’s right, even blue/green, linear, and canary deployments. We developed these service deployment lifecycle hooks with customization in mind, so we created specific integration points to shift your application traffic. You can control the behavior by writing your own logic, and Amazon ECS invokes a lifecycle hook at the production traffic-shift stage. Just note that this stage takes a Lambda target, since pause hooks can’t be configured there.

Which strategy should you pick?

Here’s the short version of everything above:

Pick a strategy

Whichever deployment strategy you choose, the guardrails (alarms, circuit breaker, lifecycle hooks, and rollback) come with the service. Configure them once, and spend your engineering time on your product, not your pipeline.

Pick one service, turn on blue/green with a CloudWatch alarm, and see for yourself. The Amazon ECS lifecycle hooks guide is a good next step once you want custom checks.

item.title: Agent security is product security, and your marketing site counts
item.dc:creator: Ankit Agrawal
item.description:
A marketing site used to have two kinds of visitors: people and search crawlers. Now an agent can build a

The post Agent security is product security, and your marketing site counts appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
A marketing site used to have two kinds of visitors: people and search crawlers. Now an agent can build a page, a second agent can scrape it, a third can summarize it for a potential customer, and a fourth can optimize it overnight after studying yesterday’s traffic. 

“The ones that you do not control make the marketing site a product with agent users, and products need product security.”

You control some of these agents but not all the data they ingest and train on. The ones that you do not control make the marketing site a product with agent users, and products need product security. A marketing site is usually public with no login required to view or break. Adversaries go after whether the site still says what you wrote, serves what you built, and reports what real visitors did. This article calls those content integrity, delivery integrity, and signal integrity, and looks at where each kind of agent touches them.

Five agents, three kinds of integrity

Five agent roles show up on a marketing site today, agents that:

  • build,
  • read or scrape,
  • analyze its visitor data,
  • optimize the site from that data, 
  • adversarial agents that attack

Each role touches at least one of three things worth protecting the integrity of:

  • Content – what the site says and links to.
  • Delivery – how that content reaches a browser, including DNS, redirects, third-party scripts, hosting, and the publish pipeline.
  • Signal – the visitor and behavior data the site produces, plus every decision made from it.

Because the content is public, the checks that matter are integrity checks. An agent with write access can be talked into making unapproved changes, so you need governance over what it may touch and logs that show what it did.

Agents that build sites

Builders are usually the first agents a team adopts, so they set the pattern for every agent that follows. A builder agent writes pages, config, scripts, and redirects. The risk sits in what it reads before it writes. A doc, a ticket, a scraped competitor page, or a CMS field can carry instructions, and an agent can follow them.

Recent incidents show the shape of this. In July 2025, someone slipped a destructive prompt into a pull request for the Amazon Q Developer extension for VS Code, and it shipped in a production version. AWS removed it and said no customer resources were affected, and reports indicate a formatting error kept the prompt from running. The same month, a Replit coding agent reportedly deleted a production database during a code freeze, despite instructions not to change anything. Replit’s response was to separate development and production databases automatically. The causes differ from provenance checks to agents stepping outside their boundaries.

The incidents above failed at different stages of Figure 2. Amazon Q failed at the input and review stages, where untrusted text in a pull request reached a trusted release. Replit failed at the harness, where an instruction to freeze changes was the only barrier between the agent and a production database. A marketing site has the same exposure, and three layers around the agent carry those controls.

  • The agentic SDLC is the process – where agents act across plan, draft, review, and publish, and which stages need a human decision.
  • The agent harness is the control layer – the code around the model that decides which tools the agent can call, with which credentials, and what gets logged or approved.
  • The sandbox is the containment layer – an isolated runtime with no standing credentials, restricted network egress, and no path to production data.

For a marketing site, that translates into a few working rules.

  • Give builder agents draft access and keep publishing behind a person.
  • Review a diff of content, scripts, and redirects. A summary written by the agent describes what it believes it did.
  • Treat every input as untrusted, including your own docs and tickets, because anyone who can edit them can steer the agent.
  • Add provenance records – which agent changed which page, from which inputs.

Webflow’s AI site builder drafts a multi-page site and design system from a prompt. The Webflow MCP server connects AI tools like Claude to a site, so an agent can design, build, and manage it through natural conversation or agentic workflows.

“Treat every input as untrusted, including your own docs and tickets, because anyone who can edit them can steer the agent.”

Webflow’s controls map to the rules above. Agent Instructions give an agent your design system, voice, CMS, and policies as skills and rules stored with your site, and agents should read them before they act. They guide an agent but don’t enforce anything, and an agent follows them as an input, so edit access matters: only Site managers and Designers can change them, and new ones stay off until someone reviews and turns them on. To see what an agent is doing, agent presence shows where any agent connected through the Webflow MCP server is working on the canvas, the same way you’d see a teammate. For the record afterward, the Site Activity Log for enterprise labels each change as Human, Webflow AI, or MCP.

Site roles do the enforcing. They let a team give a builder a narrow role, such as a Marketer with publishing switched off. That role can build pages from components but can’t publish, create API tokens, or open custom code. On Enterprise plans, design approvals go further. A role without the “Edit main site without approval” permission works in page branches, and its changes reach the main site only after required reviewers approve them.

Source by Webflow, now in research preview, is a new platform purpose-built for teams and agents to drive growth on the web, together. Source’s site-building agents work directly on your codebase. It’s designed to let teams decide how much autonomy those agents have, from requiring human approval for every change to giving agents more freedom for lower-risk work, and to hold agent actions to the same roles, permissions, and review systems as human work, with a record of what changed and which agent changed it.

Agents that read and scrape the site

Search is turning into answers, and answers are built from your pages. Agents read page text as context, and a page can contain text no visitor sees. In August 2025, Brave researchers hid instructions behind a spoiler tag in a Reddit comment. When a user asked Perplexity’s Comet browser to summarize the page, Comet followed them and exfiltrated a one-time password. Perplexity patched the issue. Any field attackers can write to on your site, such as comments, reviews, form-fed content, or CMS entries, can carry the same kind of payload to every agent that reads it.

The agent also might not see the same page you do. Researchers at SPLX showed that a site can check the user agent and serve AI crawlers different content than it serves browsers. The same technique works against you if an attacker gains write access to your site: they can change what AI systems say about you while every human check looks clean. Monitor what agents see, not only what browsers see.

Before you can control which agents read your site, you need to see them. AI bots don’t show up in standard visitor analytics, so most teams have no record of which ones visit or what they request. Webflow’s LLM bot insights fills that gap with data from your site’s server logs, so it covers the bots it tracks whether or not visitor tracking is on. It groups each bot by purpose: agentic bots that fetch pages live to answer a user’s question, training bots that collect content for model development, indexing bots that map pages for retrieval, and bots with more than one purpose. You can view activity for the whole site or a single page, filter by provider or category, and export the data as a CSV.

That gives you a baseline. Bots often focus on different pages than human visitors do, and a jump or drop after you publish is easy to spot. A page that agents fetch heavily is also a page where tampered content or injected text reaches the most readers, which makes it a good place to start the integrity checks below. The view covers named LLM bots. It doesn’t flag traffic as hostile, and it doesn’t show a user’s original query or whether a page was cited.

Visibility tells you who is there. What to do about them is a separate decision, because scrapers differ in intent. An indexer that maps your pages for retrieval and a collector that copies them for training both read public content, and you may want to allow one and not the other. Scrapers that hit your endpoints at volume add hosting cost and can slow the site for real visitors, and they count as traffic in your analytics unless something classifies them. A robots.txt file states your preference but doesn’t enforce it. Set a policy for each purpose, enforce it with rate limits and bot rules, and carry the classification into analytics so scraper traffic is reported separately from human visitors.

Agents that analyze visitor data

Analysis agents work with the most sensitive data on the site: behavior tied to real people. Webflow shows what this looks like in practice. Webflow Analyze records click events, sessions, bounce rate, time on page, and audience attributes such as traffic source, region, and device. Teams can connect an AI tool to the Webflow MCP server and ask about their site’s traffic and engagement, including page-level data, goals, and filtered results, without opening Analyze. That connected tool is an analysis agent.

The shape of the data limits what the agent can expose. Analyze uses anonymous identifiers and, according to Webflow, collects no personally identifiable information, and it relies on local storage instead of cookies. This is the setup the controls below call for: an agent that reads an anonymized dataset, not raw visitor records. If you build your own analysis agents, keep sensitive identifiers out of their context, run them in a sandbox, and give them read-only access.

Two things still need your attention. The first is consent. Analyze lets you choose always-on, opt-in, or opt-out tracking, and the opt-in and opt-out methods need a consent management solution to work properly. The tracking method decides which visitors are in the data, so the consent choices you apply belong in the dataset before an agent reads it. The second is signal quality. An analysis agent reports what the site counted, and it learns from the same signal that attackers can pollute. Label automated traffic before it reaches the agent, so it can report human and agent traffic separately. Blended answers describe bots as much as people.

Optimization agents close the loop

Optimization agents turn signal into action. They rewrite headlines, reorder sections, and adjust audiences from traffic data. That makes signal integrity a content integrity problem. If an agent learns from poisoned traffic, it ships a confident change based on bad data, and the changed page produces more skewed data for the next round.

A person who sees a conversion spike from a country you don’t sell in asks questions. An agent ships the variant. The fix is to make the loop checkable: validate the signal before an agent acts on it, hold out traffic the agent can’t tune, and require approval and rollback for changes to live pages.

“If an agent learns from poisoned traffic, it ships a confident change based on bad data, and the changed page produces more skewed data for the next round.”

Webflow Optimize shows where this loop exists in a product. An optimization has a target goal, and its variations can be tested with a traditional A/B/n split, shown by personalization rules, or handled by an AI-optimized mode that uses machine learning to serve the best-performing variation and adapt as visitor behavior shifts. That last mode is the loop in Figure 3: whatever counts as a conversion becomes the signal the system learns from, so automated traffic that completes the goal action can push a weaker variation forward. A variation can also redirect a visitor to a different page, which puts redirect destinations in scope for the delivery checks above. For teams using these features, treat the target goal as a security decision. Pick goals that bots find hard to fake, separate automated traffic from human results, and have a person review results before an AI-optimized variation becomes the default.

Agents that attack the site

A marketing site does not require a login to view its public content. Attackers go after integrity: they attempt to change what the site says, hijack what it serves, or corrupt what it reports. Automation already does this at scale, and agents lower the cost further. In testing by hCaptcha’s threat group, browser agents run against 20 common abuse scenarios attempted nearly every malicious request without any jailbreaking. Most block attempts failed because the tool lacked the capability.

Content

Content attacks change what visitors read, or send them to a copy of your site. In July 2025, Okta reported that attackers were using Vercel’s v0, a tool that builds web pages from natural-language prompts, to clone sign-in pages for brands including Microsoft 365 and cryptocurrency companies. Okta’s researchers reproduced the attack with a single prompt asking for a copy of their own login page, and Axios reported it can take as little as 30 seconds. Vercel restricted access to the sites Okta identified. The same approach can reproduce a marketing site.

Agents that run on your site raise a related problem, and the attacker doesn’t have to be an agent. In December 2023, a visitor talked the chatbot on a Chevrolet dealership’s site into agreeing to buy a new Tahoe for $1 and calling it a legally binding offer. In February 2024, a Canadian tribunal ordered Air Canada to pay $812.02 after its chatbot gave a customer wrong bereavement fare information. The tribunal wrote that “it makes no difference whether the information comes from a static page or a chatbot.” It treated the chatbot’s words as the company’s words.

Platforms carry part of the response. Webflow’s Acceptable Use Policy prohibits using the platform for impersonation, fraud, malware, and content altered to mislead people, and Webflow’s Trust and Safety team removes sites that break it. Removals come from automated detection and from reports, and ~1000 sites are taken down each day. If you find a site impersonating yours on Webflow, you can report it through the form linked in the policy or at abuse@webflow.com.

Delivery

Delivery attacks hijack the path between your content and the visitor’s browser, and they don’t need to touch your page. In 2024, a company acquired the polyfill.io domain and changed the script it served, which redirected mobile visitors on more than 100,000 sites to scam pages. The site owners hadn’t changed a line of code, and Google began warning advertisers whose landing pages loaded the script. A week after the disclosure, Censys still counted nearly 385,000 hosts referencing the domain, including 182 government sites.

DNS follows the same pattern. Guardio Labs found more than 8,000 domains and 13,000 subdomains tied to well-known brands hijacked through dangling CNAME and SPF records, then used to send about five million emails a day under those brands’ names. Open redirects borrow a trusted domain’s reputation the same way. Cofense found that every US .gov domain abused in phishing campaigns between November 2022 and November 2024 was used for an open redirect, and KnowBe4 documented a 2025 campaign against finance and healthcare organizations that relied on open redirects in legitimate services.

Agents make the search for these cheaper. Finding a dangling record or a redirect parameter is a scanning problem, and agent tooling can follow a hit through to a tailored phishing page faster than a script could.

Signal

Signal attacks corrupt what the site reports. Fake form fills, synthetic sessions, and scripted browsing pollute analytics, attribution, and audiences. The scale is real: Imperva’s 2025 Bad Bot Report found that automated traffic reached 51% of web traffic in 2024, and bad bots accounted for 37%. Forms are the most direct path from a bot into a marketing team’s CRM, so they are a good place to start. Webflow’s form spam protection offers four methods that you can combine. The reCAPTCHA field asks visitors to identify themselves as human before they submit, although Webflow notes that it can hurt user experience and that more advanced bots can get around it. A site-level bot blocking setting uses AI to analyze mouse movements, inputs, and other signals, and blocks submissions from bots on every form on the site. A second site-level setting, spam filtering, checks all the form data sent on your site and filters out spam submissions. The honeypot technique adds a hidden field that real visitors never fill in, so a filled field marks the submission as spam. Because the CAPTCHA can be circumvented, none of these should carry the load alone.

The damage reaches visitors too. A visitor’s history is the record that drives what they see next. When synthetic sessions merge into real audiences, or identities get stitched together wrongly, retargeting and personalization act on the wrong history, and real visitors get irrelevant offers.

How to secure your marketing site against agents

The controls differ by layer, but the first step is the same for all three: list every agent that touches your site, including the ones you don’t operate. You can’t protect a layer from an agent you haven’t counted.

Content. Review agent-authored changes like code. Keep a record of which agent changed what and from which inputs, and alert on diffs nobody requested. Fetch key pages with common AI crawler user agents and compare the result to what a browser gets.

Delivery. Allowlist redirect destinations, and remove any endpoint that redirects to an arbitrary URL. Audit DNS for dangling CNAME records and SPF includes that point at services you no longer use. Keep an inventory of third-party scripts, and apply Subresource Integrity or serve them from your own origin where you can. The polyfill.io incident is the case for it.

Signal. Classify automated traffic before it reaches analytics. Rate-limit and validate form submissions, and layer the protections your platform offers, such as bot blocking, spam filtering, and a honeypot field. Tag agent-originated sessions so they stay out of human audiences and human-focused tests, and report on them as their own segment.

Across all of it. Apply least privilege to every agent, keep logs you can query, and put a person in front of the publish step.

Your marketing site now has more kinds of visitors, and some of them can edit it.

If an agent changed what your site says tonight, would you know which one it was, what it read first, and who approved the change?

This article was originally published on November 10, 2026, on webflow.com.

Your marketing site now has AI agent visitors and editors. Learn how to secure content, delivery, and signal integrity against threats.

item.title: Groundcover Investigations lets engineers steer AI SRE agents
item.dc:creator: Meredith Shubel
item.description:
Groundcover, the eBPF-based observability startup, has introduced Investigations, giving agents and engineers one place to collaborate on incident response in

The post Groundcover Investigations lets engineers steer AI SRE agents appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Groundcover, the eBPF-based observability startup, has introduced Investigations, giving agents and engineers one place to collaborate on incident response in real time. 

In the shared workspace, groundcover’s investigator and moderator agents work with on-call engineers and their preferred coding agents to investigate production incidents together, analyzing behavior across applications and infrastructure to create a shared record of evidence. 

Rather than handing full control to agents, the idea is to help engineers and agents work together on incident investigations.

“Most AI SRE tools ask engineers to step back and let the agent take over. We built Investigations for engineers to step in.”

Shahar Azulay, CEO and co-founder at groundcover, tells The New Stack that “Most AI SRE tools ask engineers to step back and let the agent take over. We built Investigations for engineers to step in.” 

Everyone has their favorite agent. That’s a problem 

AI agents are flooding daily software engineering workflows. Already, Salesforce reports that organizations use an average of 12 agents — a number that’s expected to grow by 67% within two years. But half of those agents are working in silos.

This presents a particular problem in incident response. Individual agents, like Claude Code or Codex, may be able to troubleshoot on their own, but how can engineers aggregate their findings? They don’t — or at least, it’s very tricky. More often than not, Azulay says agents’ varying conclusions are spread across chats and tickets. 

As he describes it: “Every engineer now has an agent, but each of those agents investigates on its own and findings end up in a chat window.” 

How groundcover wants engineers and agents to work together

With its Investigations, groundcover aims to eliminate fragmented incident response and create a single source of truth for every engineer and agent. Here, agents can lead collaborative, evidence-driven investigations, testing hypotheses against production data, validating findings, and backing every conclusion with evidence. Engineers, for their part, get real-time visibility into the investigation and can step in to steer it as they see fit. 

It all starts when a monitor issue fires and an engineer opens an investigation from groundcover or Slack. groundcover says automatically opening an investigation when a monitor fires is coming next.

The investigator agent builds a graph with a question (e.g., Why is checkout latency spiking in the US?) and then opens several hypotheses to explain it. From there, it turns to production telemetry to query the traces, logs, metrics, and Kubernetes events the groundcover eBPF sensor is already collecting, testing each one and recording what it finds as evidence. 

Importantly, Azulay tells The New Stack, “the investigator can’t mark its own work as correct. When it thinks a hypothesis is supported, it submits a proposal that cites specific findings, and a separate agent, the moderator, acts as an LLM-as-a-judge and checks whether that evidence backs up the claim. No findings, no closure.”

“Separating the agent that does the work from the agent that judges it gives you a conclusion you can trust without redoing every step.”

Given the speed at which agents reach conclusions — and the risk that they act beyond scope — Azulay says this separation of hypothesis and conclusion is crucial to arriving at a trustworthy conclusion: “Separating the agent that does the work from the agent that judges it gives you a conclusion you can trust without redoing every step.” 

According to groundcover, the investigator agent also learns from each investigation so it can understand which hypotheses tend to hold up and where to look first when similar problems arise.

External coding agents are invited to the party, too

While groundcover’s investigator and moderator agents lead investigations, the startup recognizes that most engineers already bring a slew of third-party agents to the table, whether for business intelligence, coding, product roadmapping, etc. Those agents are welcome in Investigations, too.

Using groundcover’s MCP server, engineers can connect Claude Code, Codex, and other agents to the shared workspace to read and add to the same investigation. That builds on groundcover’s October launch, which let outside coding agents query its telemetry over MCP and hand off investigations to groundcover’s own agent. 

For Azulay, this lets each agent shine in what it does best. As he tells The New Stack: 

“Coding agents and groundcover’s agents are good at different things. Our agents know your telemetry and how to query it fast. Your coding agents know your code. Neither has the full picture.” 

Working together, then, via Investigations, the different agents can lean on each other depending on the task at hand. If a hypothesis points to a code problem, for example, the investigator agent may bring in Claude Code or Codex to check it. When engineers’ coding agent needs telemetry, groundcover’s agent fetches the data. 

“Our agents know your telemetry and how to query it fast. Your coding agents know your code. Neither has the full picture.”

What matters is that every agent publishes its findings in the same investigation tree, preventing engineers from going on a wild goose chase trying to connect the dots across five different private chat sessions. 

“Everyone can see what’s been checked, what’s still open, and why anyone believes what they believe,” says Azulay. “Every contribution is attributed, so you know a finding came from a specific engineer’s Claude session at a specific time.” 

Does this mean agents and engineers are on even footing? 

Not quite. Per Omer Mayer, senior product manager, groundcover, engineers can “watch each hypothesis get supported or ruled out in real time” — and they can “step in and steer it” at any time. 

In other words, engineers can immediately see what groundcover agents are investigating. If they think the agents are off the mark, they can easily take over.

Azulay offers The New Stack an example: Suppose a checkout latency monitor fires, and an automated investigation kicks off, generating three hypotheses, one of which is a slow query from a recent deploy.

But the on-call engineer knows something the investigator agent doesn’t: The deploy was rolled back 10 minutes earlier and latency didn’t recover. Easy — they can stop that hypothesis, which closes everything under it and tells the agent to stop spending time and tokens there. 

“The engineer might also add context the agents don’t have, like ‘the payments team changed their retry policy this morning,’” adds Azulay. “That opens a new line of inquiry nobody would have found in the telemetry alone.”

What’s also important is engineers’ right to override where agents can’t. Remember, the investigator agent is forbidden from closing anything without the moderator agent’s okay. But engineers don’t need the moderator’s permission to steer the investigation, Azulay says.

“The moderator is there to keep the agents honest, not to slow down the people responsible for the incident,” says Azulay. 

More agents are teaming up

Earlier this year, more vendors made moves to bring individual agents out of isolated workflows and into a shared space. 

On the coding side, Cognition, Microsoft, and Augment Code all launched team-layer coding agent platforms, pushing coding agents past the single-developer loop. 

Last month, Harness acquired select Augment Code assets, including Cosmos, to link AI coding agents to its delivery platform. This way, teams writing code in Cosmos will have context from across the software development lifecycle available to the agent as it works.

Now, groundcover’s Investigations brings a similar shared-space principle to incident response. More work is happening elsewhere, too. Slack Code has given coding agents their own temporary channels for plans, diffs, and live previews, which Katie Steigman, vice president of product at Slack, told The New Stack is already being used for incident response.

Other companies are also building tools for collaborative incident investigations, including shared workspaces for engineers and agents and handoffs to coding agents over MCP.

So far, conversations have focused on agents’ individual prowess and what they can do. But as agents move deeper into software engineering workflows, agent-engineer teamwork looks like what will make incident response work best. 

The post Groundcover Investigations lets engineers steer AI SRE agents appeared first on The New Stack.
Every engineer now has an AI agent, but each one investigates alone. groundcover is betting on a shared workspace where agents and engineers work together.

item.title: Why groundcover’s CEO says agents are the power users of observability
item.dc:creator: Chris J. Preimesberger
item.description:
An AI coding agent can write a patch in minutes. Ask it whether that patch slows down the API endpoint

The post Why groundcover’s CEO says agents are the power users of observability appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
An AI coding agent can write a patch in minutes. Ask it whether that patch slows down the API endpoint your customers hit most, and suddenly it needs something that lives outside the repository. It needs to see how the software runs.

That’s the premise behind groundcover, an observability platform that wants to put production telemetry in the hands of developers and their coding agents. Yes, you read that correctly.

In a conversation with The New Stack’s Frederic Lardinois at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon this month in Salt Lake City, groundcover CEO and co-founder Shahar Azulay explained why he thinks the same data engineers use to troubleshoot an incident can help an agent write and test a better change in the first place.

Your new observability user is an agent

“Now agents are the power users of observability,” Azulay told TNS. 

Groundcover exposes telemetry through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), giving coding agents a way to query it while they work. An agent investigating a slow API, for example, could use traces to see which service accounts for most of the latency. A developer writing a test could use observed application behavior to pick a scenario customers actually encounter.

Groundcover uses that approach internally. Its coding agents pull context from the company’s own telemetry, and agents involved in code review can look at measurements from staging deployments. It’s a way to give a reviewer something concrete to check when a patch looks perfectly reasonable in a diff.

Agents also give engineers something new to monitor. Azulay contrasts a familiar application trace that follows a request across several microservices with an agent run that can span hours and thousands of tool calls. A trace that long can make a Kubernetes incident look like light reading. 

Developers may need to inspect prompts and tool calls or use evaluations to judge whether a run behaved as intended. A completed run tells you the agent stopped. The trace can help you figure out what it did along the way.

Less instrumentation work, more room for detail

Groundcover uses an eBPF sensor to collect application and infrastructure telemetry without requiring developers to add an SDK to every service. It also supports OpenTelemetry, so teams can keep sending the signals they already collect and add custom instrumentation where they need more detail. That gives developers a baseline for a new service and a way to get more specific when a particular path or business operation warrants it.

Where the data runs is part of the pitch. Groundcover’s bring-your-own-cloud model keeps telemetry and groundcover’s agent operations in the customer’s cloud environment, Azulay said. Customers pay for the underlying infrastructure, and groundcover manages the deployment. 

For teams weighing how much telemetry to retain, the model puts the infrastructure bill in their own account. It also matters when prompts or tool calls may contain sensitive customer data and teams want to keep that information under their control.

We also ask what happens when the platform starts acting on what it sees. Azulay points to groundcover’s move into Kubernetes optimization, where the immediate work centers on cost and resilience. He sees a path from there to agents that can help address an incident on both sides of the deployment, proposing a code change and adjusting infrastructure configuration. The conversation also gets into the practical work of switching observability platforms, including what happens to the dashboards and monitors engineers have spent years building.

Watch the full KubeCon interview on The New Stack’s YouTube channel to hear how groundcover uses its own telemetry in code reviews and why Azulay thinks the next generation of coding agents will be a regular part of the observability stack.

The post Why groundcover’s CEO says agents are the power users of observability appeared first on The New Stack.

AI coding agents can write code, but can they tell how it performs? The New Stack interviewed groundcover CEO Shahar Azulay about giving agents access to production telemetry to help them investigate problems, review patches and write better tests.

item.title: Google’s Gemini 4 Neon tripled its coding score without changing the model
item.dc:creator: Amanda Caswell
item.description:
Google’s new Gemini 4 Neon resolved 12.8% of the SWE-sweep coding benchmark using the mini-SWE harness, but that score jumped

The post Google’s Gemini 4 Neon tripled its coding score without changing the model appeared first on The New Stack.
item.content:encoded:
Google’s new Gemini 4 Neon resolved 12.8% of the SWE-sweep coding benchmark using the mini-SWE harness, but that score jumped to 39.0% when the same model ran inside Antigravity.

The more-than-threefold improvement raises questions about how much coding-agent performance comes from the underlying model and how much depends on the harness…

Both results were reported Wednesday as part of the Neon launch. The more-than-threefold improvement raises questions about how much coding-agent performance comes from the underlying model and how much depends on the harness managing its tools, context, and execution.

A day earlier, a FrontierHarness benchmark found that running the same open model could cost up to five times more depending on the harness

Same model, different scores

Google’s Gemini 4 Neon model card compares three frontier models on SWE-sweep using their respective provider harnesses and a shared mini-SWE baseline.

Neon and Opus performed substantially better with their providers’ harnesses, but Sol did not.

Claude Opus 5.5 climbed from 3.6% with mini-SWE to 10.1% with Claude Code, while GPT-6.2 Sol went the other way, falling from 11.6% with mini-SWE to 8.3% with Codex. Neon and Opus performed substantially better with their providers’ harnesses, but Sol did not.

Google tested each model in two harness configurations, though the comparison does not isolate which changes account for the differences or whether the results would hold up across other benchmarks and repositories.

The harness does the work

Antigravity’s harness was co-trained with Gemini, and Neon has been updated to make fewer unnecessary file reads and better manage context during long coding sessions. Antigravity can also run subagents in separate Git worktrees and verify their changes.

Google only tested Neon against mini-SWE, so there’s no data yet on how it performs with other harnesses.

It’s unclear which of those changes contributed most to the SWE-sweep improvement, since they weren’t tested separately. Google only tested Neon against mini-SWE, so there’s no data yet on how it performs with other harnesses.

Neon plans, Hydrogen builds

Neon is joining the model-switching system Google introduced with Gemini 4 Hydrogen. It handles planning and harder coding problems, leaving routine work to Hydrogen, and can run multiple Hydrogen subagents in parallel using the /swarm feature introduced with Carbon.

Google hasn’t said how much this setup affects Neon’s SWE-sweep results or what it means for the cost of completing a task.

Counting the cost per task

The company reports that Neon scored 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1 and 46.2% on FrontierCode 2.0 at its default high reasoning setting. It also topped the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with a score of 58.6.

At its default high thinking level, the model costs 32% less per task than Gemini 4 Carbon, according to Google’s comparison using the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. API pricing is $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, with cached input at $0.15 per million tokens and a 1 million-token context window.

Neon is available through the Gemini API, Google AI Studio, and Gemini for Business. Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers can also access it through Antigravity.
